title: Branching Workflows: Rebase vs Merge, Code Review & MRs
summary: Master Git branching workflows — when to merge, when to rebase, how to resolve conflicts — and how to run rigorous merge-request reviews, including the dependency-pinning requirements.txt review exercise drawn from real panel interviews.
objectives: Explain the difference between merge and rebase and choose the right one for shared versus private branches.
Resolve merge conflicts during both merges and rebases using the standard edit-stage-continue workflow.
Describe fast-forward merges and decide when to preserve topology with --no-ff.
Conduct a merge-request review that checks correctness, scope, tests, secrets, and dependency hygiene.
Review a requirements.txt change and justify an approve versus request-changes verdict based on version pinning.

notes.title: Merge: joining two histories with a merge commit
notes.body:
A merge takes the tips of two branches, finds their common ancestor (the merge base), combines the changes from both sides, and records the result as a merge commit — a commit with two parents. That two-parent commit is the permanent record that "these two lines of work came together here." Worked example: you branched feature/login off main, and while you worked, main also moved forward, so the histories diverged. You finish and run:

$ git checkout main
$ git merge feature/login

Git cannot fast-forward (covered in the next note), so it creates a merge commit. `git log --graph --oneline` now shows:

*   9f3a2c1 Merge branch 'feature/login'
|\
| * 7b1e04d Add login form
| * 2c8f9aa Validate email input
|/
* 4d5aa10 Deploy pipeline fix

Solution walkthrough: main sat at 4d5aa10 while feature/login added 2c8f9aa and 7b1e04d on its own line. The merge commit 9f3a2c1 has two parents — 4d5aa10 and 7b1e04d — and its content is the union of both sides. If both sides touched the same lines, Git stops and asks you to resolve conflicts (see the conflicts note). Merging never rewrites existing commits: every commit keeps its original hash, which is why merge is always safe on shared branches. The trade-off is a busier graph — long-lived projects accumulate many merge commits, which is exactly the problem rebasing solves.

notes.title: Rebase: replaying your commits onto a new base
notes.body:
Rebasing takes your branch's commits, temporarily sets them aside, moves your branch pointer to the tip of the target branch, then re-applies your commits one by one on top — as if you had started your work from the latest main all along. The result is a perfectly linear history with no merge commit. Worked example: your private branch feature/login is three commits behind a fast-moving main:

$ git checkout feature/login
$ git fetch origin
$ git rebase origin/main

If main added commits A and B while you added X and Y, your history goes from `...-A-B` plus a side line `X-Y` to a single line `...-A-B-X'-Y'`. The primes matter: X' and Y' are NEW commits with new hashes, because their parent changed. That rewriting is the whole point and the whole danger. Solution check: after rebasing, run `git log --oneline --graph` and confirm a single straight line, then run your tests — rebased code can break if main changed an API you depend on. Because hashes change, anyone else holding the old X and Y now has divergent history. Hence the golden rule of rebasing: never rebase commits that exist on a shared branch other people may have pulled. Rebase private branches freely; merge shared ones. A common safe pattern is `git pull --rebase`, which rebases only your own unpushed commits on top of what you just fetched.

notes.title: Fast-forward merges: when history is already linear
notes.body:
A fast-forward is not really a merge at all — it happens when the branch you are merging is directly ahead of your current branch with no divergence. Git simply slides the branch pointer forward; no merge commit is created and no conflict is possible. Worked example: you cut a hotfix branch from main, committed one fix, and main has not moved since:

$ git checkout main
$ git log --oneline -2
4d5aa10 Deploy pipeline fix
$ git merge hotfix/timeout
Updating 4d5aa10..a91c3e2
Fast-forward
 app.py | 2 +-

Solution walkthrough: hotfix/timeout's tip a91c3e2 is a direct descendant of 4d5aa10, so Git just moves the main pointer to a91c3e2. `git log --graph` stays a straight line — there is no evidence a branch ever existed. That cleanliness is sometimes exactly what you do NOT want: for release branches or long-running feature branches, teams often prefer a merge commit marking the integration point, so the branch's scope stays visible. That is what `git merge --no-ff` is for — it forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible:

$ git merge --no-ff hotfix/timeout -m "Merge hotfix/timeout: raise API timeout"

Many teams set branch policies (GitHub "require merge commit" or squash policies) to standardize this. Panel tip: if asked "what is a fast-forward," answer with the condition — the target branch contains your branch's tip as an ancestor — not just "it moves the pointer."

notes.title: Resolving conflicts: one workflow for merge and rebase
notes.body:
A conflict means both sides changed the same lines (or one side deleted what the other edited) and Git cannot choose for you. The resolution workflow is identical in spirit for merges and rebases; only the command that resumes differs. Worked example: main sets `timeout = 30` while your branch sets `timeout = 60` on the same line. During `git merge`, Git stops and marks the file:

<<<<<<< HEAD
timeout = 30
=======
timeout = 60
>>>>>>> feature/login

Solution, step by step. First, `git status` to see which files are conflicted — never guess. Second, open each file and decide the correct content; here the right answer might be neither literal value but `timeout = 45` with a comment, or keeping one side. Delete the marker lines entirely. Third, `git add` the resolved files to mark them resolved. Fourth, finish: for a merge, run `git commit` (Git pre-fills the merge message — keep it); for a rebase, run `git rebase --continue` to replay the remaining commits. If you get lost, `git merge --abort` or `git rebase --abort` restores everything to the pre-operation state — aborting is always safe and is the correct answer when a rebase conflict spirals. Two professional habits: resolve conflicts in small chunks (rebase one commit at a time with `git rebase -i` when the branch is long), and after resolving, run the test suite before continuing — a "resolved" conflict that breaks tests is worse than an unresolved one.

notes.title: Code review that catches real problems
notes.body:
A merge-request review is a correctness gate, not a style debate. Work through this checklist on every MR, in order. One: does the change do what the title claims, and nothing more? Scope creep — a "fix timeout" MR that also refactors logging — gets sent back. Two: are there tests, and do they fail without the fix? Three: are secrets, tokens, or credentials anywhere in the diff, including in test fixtures and config examples? A leaked secret means blocking the MR and rotating the secret, not just deleting the line. Four: dependencies — every new package needs a pinned version and a reason (see the next note). Five: backwards compatibility — does this break existing callers, configs, or stored data? Worked example of review infrastructure: a CODEOWNERS file auto-assigns the right reviewers so security-sensitive paths never slip through unreviewed:

# CODEOWNERS
/terraform/      @platform-team
/docker/         @platform-team @security-team
/requirements*.txt @platform-team

With this file, any MR touching /terraform/ automatically requests the platform team. The review verdicts are approve (ship it), comment (feedback, author decides), and request changes (do not merge until addressed) — requesting changes on an unpinned dependency or a hardcoded secret is the panel-expected answer, and you should be able to defend it out loud in under a minute.

notes.title: Panel exercise: review this requirements.txt MR
notes.body:
This is the dependency-review exercise panels actually give: an MR adds a requirements.txt and you must approve or request changes. Here is an original example in that spirit. The MR adds:

requests
flask
flask-cors
asyncio
setuptools
pandas
pytest

Verdict: request changes — and here is the full solution with reasoning for each line. First, every production dependency is unpinned. Unpinned installs resolve to whatever is newest on install day, so builds are not reproducible: the artifact you tested is not the artifact you deploy. Pin with == after verifying the versions work (example pins: requests==2.32.3, flask==3.1.0, flask-cors==5.0.0, pandas==2.2.3). Second, asyncio is part of the Python standard library — listing it in requirements.txt is wrong; remove the line (pip will simply fail to find it or confuse readers). Third, setuptools is a build backend, not a runtime dependency of the application — remove it from the runtime file. Fourth, pytest is a test dependency and does not belong in the production install; move it to a separate requirements-test.txt (example pin: pytest==8.3.3) so production images stay lean and the attack surface stays small. The corrected requirements.txt is four pinned runtime lines, and the review comment lists each finding with its fix. In the panel, say the verdict first, then walk the lines — verdict-first is what interviewers score.

cards.front: What is the fundamental difference between git merge and git rebase?
cards.back: Merge preserves both histories and records the join with a merge commit (two parents); rebase rewrites your commits as new commits replayed linearly on top of the target branch, producing straight-line history but changing commit hashes.

cards.front: State the golden rule of rebasing.
cards.back: Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared branch other people may have pulled — rewriting public history orphans everyone else's copies.

cards.front: When does git merge do a fast-forward instead of creating a merge commit?
cards.back: When the branch being merged is directly ahead of the current branch (your tip is an ancestor of its tip) — Git just slides the pointer forward with no new commit.

cards.front: How do you force a merge commit when a fast-forward is possible?
cards.back: git merge --no-ff <branch> — used to keep an explicit integration marker for release or feature branches.

cards.front: What do the <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>> markers in a conflicted file mean?
cards.back: They delimit the two competing versions: content between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is your current branch's version; between ======= and >>>>>>> is the incoming branch's version.

cards.front: After resolving rebase conflicts, which command continues the rebase? How do you bail out?
cards.back: git rebase --continue resumes replaying commits; git rebase --abort restores the branch to its pre-rebase state safely.

cards.front: What is a CODEOWNERS file and why does it matter?
cards.back: It maps file paths to owning teams/users so the right reviewers are auto-requested on every MR — ensuring security-sensitive paths (Terraform, Docker, dependencies) are never merged unreviewed.

cards.front: An MR adds unpinned dependencies (e.g. a bare 'flask' line). Approve or request changes?
cards.back: Request changes — unpinned versions make builds non-reproducible; pin every runtime dependency with == after verifying.

cards.front: An MR's requirements.txt lists 'asyncio'. What is your review finding?
cards.back: asyncio is in the Python standard library and must not be a pip requirement — remove the line.

cards.front: An MR puts pytest in the production requirements.txt. What do you require?
cards.back: Move it to a separate test requirements file — test tooling does not belong in the production install (leaner images, smaller attack surface).

cards.front: What does git pull --rebase do, and why is it safe?
cards.back: It fetches, then replays only your own unpushed local commits on top of the fetched tip — safe because it never rewrites commits anyone else has.

cards.front: You find a hardcoded API secret in an MR diff. What are the correct actions?
cards.back: Block the MR (request changes), rotate/revoke the exposed secret immediately, and purge it from history — deleting the line alone is not enough since history retains it.

quiz.q: Panel question: what is the biggest difference between rebase and merge?
choices: Rebase is faster because it skips conflict detection
Merge rewrites commit hashes while rebase preserves them
Rebase replays commits as new commits for linear history; merge preserves both histories with a merge commit
They are identical; rebase is just an alias for merge
quiz.explain: Rebase rewrites your commits (new hashes) onto the target tip for a straight line; merge keeps every original commit and records the join point with a two-parent merge commit.

quiz.q: Which statement about the golden rule of rebasing is correct?
choices: Never rebase commits pushed to a shared branch others may have pulled
Always rebase main into your branch before pushing
quiz.explain: Rewriting public history orphans collaborators' copies; rebase is for private branches, merge is for shared ones.

quiz.q: git merge reports 'Fast-forward'. What does that tell you?
choices: Your branch tip was an ancestor of the merged branch, so Git just moved the pointer
The merge was rejected by branch policy
quiz.explain: Fast-forward means no divergence existed — the merged branch was directly ahead, so no merge commit was needed.

quiz.q: During a rebase you hit a conflict, resolve the file, and stage it. What next?
choices: git rebase --continue to replay remaining commits
quiz.explain: Staging marks the conflict resolved; --continue resumes replaying the rest of your commits onto the new base.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a CODEOWNERS file?
choices: To list who wrote each line of code
To auto-request the right reviewers for sensitive paths on every MR
To assign merge permissions in the CI pipeline
To document the team's on-call rotation
quiz.explain: CODEOWNERS maps paths to owning teams so Terraform, Docker, and dependency changes always get expert review.

quiz.q: An MR adds requirements.txt containing a bare 'requests' line with no version. Your verdict?
choices: Approve — pip always picks the safest version
Approve with a comment suggesting a version someday
Request changes — pin with == for reproducible builds
quiz.explain: Unpinned dependencies resolve differently on different days, so the tested artifact may not match the deployed one; pin versions.

quiz.q: The same MR lists 'asyncio' as a requirement. What do you tell the author?
choices: Remove it — asyncio ships with Python's standard library
Move it to the test requirements
Approve — explicit is better than implicit
quiz.explain: asyncio is stdlib; listing it as a pip dependency is incorrect and will confuse or break installs.

quiz.q: The MR includes 'pytest' in the production requirements.txt. What is the right fix?
choices: Pin pytest and keep it — tests run in production
Remove pytest entirely — testing is optional
Move pytest to a separate test requirements file
quiz.explain: Test dependencies belong in a separate requirements-test.txt so production images stay lean with a smaller attack surface.

quiz.q: Your teammate rebased the shared main branch and force-pushed. What is the consequence?
choices: Nothing — Git auto-heals on the next pull
Everyone else's local main now diverges; they must recover (e.g. re-clone or reset to the new upstream)
The old commits are permanently deleted from the server
CI pipelines run twice as fast
quiz.explain: Rewriting shared history orphans every collaborator's copy — this is exactly what the golden rule forbids.

items.prompt: Panel: 'Explain rebase versus merge to me.' Give the 60-second answer.
items.answer: Merge joins two histories with a merge commit that has two parents, preserving every original commit and hash — safe for shared branches but leaves a busier graph. Rebase replays my commits as brand-new commits on top of the target branch, giving linear history, but it rewrites hashes, so it is only for private branches.
items.explain: Hits the four scoring points: merge commit/two parents, hash preservation, rebase replay/new hashes, and the private-vs-shared rule.

items.prompt: State the golden rule of rebasing and the reason behind it.
items.answer: Never rebase commits pushed to a shared branch others may have pulled, because rewriting public history orphans every collaborator's copy and forces painful recovery.
items.explain: The rule plus the mechanism (orphaned copies) is the complete panel answer.

items.prompt: When is git merge a fast-forward, and when would you use --no-ff?
items.answer: Fast-forward happens when the merged branch is directly ahead with no divergence — Git just moves the pointer. Use --no-ff to force a merge commit that marks the integration point, e.g. for release branches where you want the branch scope visible in history.
items.explain: Condition first (ancestor check), then the deliberate --no-ff use case.

items.prompt: What does git pull --rebase do, and why is it considered safe?
items.answer: It fetches remote changes, then replays only my own unpushed local commits on top of the fetched tip. It is safe because it never rewrites commits anyone else has — only my private, unpushed work.
items.explain: Distinguishes private unpushed commits (safe to rewrite) from public ones.

items.prompt: Mid-rebase you hit a conflict. List the exact recovery commands.
items.answer: git status to identify conflicted files, edit and resolve, git add to mark resolved, git rebase --continue to resume — or git rebase --abort at any point to restore the pre-rebase state.
items.explain: The full loop including the abort escape hatch shows practiced experience.

items.prompt: Your feature branch is private and main moved ahead. Rebase or merge main in — and why?
items.answer: Rebase the private branch onto the updated main: it keeps history linear, surfaces integration issues against the latest code, and the golden rule is satisfied because the branch is private.
items.explain: Applies the decision rule rather than reciting definitions.

items.prompt: Why do many teams merge (not rebase) release branches into main?
items.answer: The merge commit permanently marks where the release line integrated, preserving the true topology of what shipped together — rebasing would flatten that record away.
items.explain: Shows judgment about history as documentation, not just mechanics.

items.prompt: What does a CODEOWNERS entry '/terraform/ @platform-team' guarantee?
items.answer: Every MR touching /terraform/ automatically requests review from the platform team, so infrastructure changes cannot merge without expert eyes.
items.explain: The value is automatic, path-scoped reviewer assignment.

items.prompt: MR adds requirements.txt with unpinned 'flask'. Verdict and reason?
items.answer: Request changes: unpinned versions make builds non-reproducible — pin with == after verifying the versions.
items.explain: Reproducibility is the core argument panels expect.

items.prompt: The same file lists 'asyncio'. Your review comment?
items.answer: Remove it — asyncio is part of the Python standard library, not a pip package.
items.explain: Tests whether the reviewer knows stdlib from third-party.

items.prompt: The file lists 'setuptools' as a runtime dependency. Your finding?
items.answer: Remove it from the runtime file — setuptools is a build backend, not something the application needs at runtime.
items.explain: Distinguishes build-time from runtime dependencies.

items.prompt: Where should 'pytest' live, and why not in production requirements?
items.answer: In a separate requirements-test.txt — test tooling in the production install bloats images and widens the attack surface for no runtime benefit.
items.explain: Separation of test and runtime dependency sets.

items.prompt: You spot a hardcoded AWS secret key in the MR diff. Exact actions?
items.answer: Request changes to block the merge, rotate/revoke the exposed key immediately, and purge it from Git history — deleting the line is insufficient.
items.explain: Block + rotate + purge; history retains anything merely deleted.

items.prompt: When do you choose 'request changes' over 'comment' on an MR?
items.answer: Request changes when the MR must not merge as-is — unpinned dependencies, secrets, missing tests, scope creep. Comment when the feedback is advisory and the author can decide.
items.explain: Shows the reviewer understands the verdict as a merge gate.

handsOnLab.title: Branch, conflict, rebase, and review
handsOnLab.brief: You will build a small Git repository from scratch, create a merge conflict and resolve it, rebase a private branch onto a moved main, enforce review ownership with CODEOWNERS, and produce a pinned requirements.txt from an unpinned MR-style starting point.
steps: Create the lab repo: run mkdir branching-lab && cd branching-lab && git init -b main, then git config user.name 'Lab Learner' and git config user.email 'learner@example.com'.
Commit a starting point: create app.py containing 'timeout = 30' on one line, then git add app.py && git commit -m 'Set default API timeout'.
Create a feature branch: git checkout -b feature/timeout, change the line to 'timeout = 60', commit with message 'Raise timeout for slow endpoint'.
Divert main: git checkout main, change the same line to 'timeout = 45  # tuned per load test', commit as 'Tune timeout per load test'.

Merge and resolve: run git merge feature/timeout, observe the conflict, open app.py, replace the marker block with your chosen final value, git add app.py, then git commit (accept the default merge message).
Verify the merge commit: run git log --graph --oneline and confirm a merge commit with two parents exists.

Rebase exercise: git checkout -b feature/retry, add a line 'retries = 3' to app.py and commit; then git checkout main, append '# main moved' comment line and commit; then git checkout feature/retry && git rebase main, and confirm git log --oneline --graph shows a straight line.
Force a merge commit: git checkout main && git merge --no-ff feature/retry -m 'Merge feature/retry', then confirm the merge commit exists even though fast-forward was possible.
Add review ownership: create a CODEOWNERS file mapping '/app.py' to your username and any '*.txt' to a second reviewer name.

Produce the pinned file: write requirements-v1.txt with unpinned lines (requests, flask, flask-cors, asyncio, setuptools, pandas, pytest), then write the corrected requirements.txt (pinned runtime deps only) and requirements-test.txt, and save a diff or notes file review-notes.md with your verdict and per-line reasoning.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A local Git repo containing the merge commit, the rebased linear section, the --no-ff merge commit, a CODEOWNERS file, requirements-v1.txt, the corrected requirements.txt + requirements-test.txt, and review-notes.md with the verdict.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: git log --graph --oneline shows both a merge commit and a straight rebased section; requirements.txt has no asyncio/setuptools/pytest lines and every runtime dep is pinned with ==; review-notes.md states 'request changes' with per-line reasons.

mockTask.q: Panel: your feature branch is private, main has moved ahead, and you are about to open an MR. What do you do?
choices: Merge main into the branch to keep all history, then open the MR
Rebase the branch onto the updated main, run tests, then open the MR
Force-push the branch onto main and skip the MR
Open the MR first and let CI resolve the divergence
mockTask.explain: The branch is private so the golden rule is satisfied; rebasing gives a clean linear history and validates the code against the latest main before review. Merging main in is for shared branches; force-pushing to main and skipping review are both disqualifying answers.

title: Python Fundamentals: Script-Reading Mastery
summary: Build rock-solid Python reading fluency — types, control flow, functions, comprehensions, and file I/O — through original predict-the-output drills in the spirit of the panel's script-reading exercise, so you can trace any automation script cold.
objectives: Predict the exact console output of short Python scripts covering loops, conditions, and data structures.
Distinguish mutable from immutable types and explain aliasing bugs.
Write and read list, dict, and set comprehensions with filters.
Use functions with default, *args, and **kwargs parameters correctly.
Read and parse text files safely with context managers and string methods.

notes.title: Dynamic typing and the mutable/immutable divide
notes.body:
Python variables are names bound to objects, not typed boxes — the same name can point at an int, then a string, then a list. What matters for bugs is whether the object itself can change in place. Immutable types (int, float, str, tuple) never change: operations on them create new objects. Mutable types (list, dict, set) can be modified through any name pointing at them, which is the classic aliasing trap. Worked example:

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)
print(a)

Solution: this prints [1, 2, 3, 4] — not [1, 2, 3]. The assignment b = a copies the reference, not the list, so both names point at the same object and the append is visible through a. The fix is an explicit copy: b = a.copy() or b = list(a). Contrast with strings:

s = "web"
t = s
t = t + "1"
print(s)

Solution: prints "web" — concatenation built a new string object and rebound only t. In DevOps scripts this divide bites when a function mutates a list or dict passed in by the caller: the caller's data changes silently. Default to copying inputs you intend to transform, and treat any shared mutable structure as suspect until proven otherwise.

notes.title: Control flow: loops, break, continue, and the loop-else
Functions: parameters, defaults, *args, **kwargs
notes.body:
A Python function signature can mix positional parameters, defaults, *args (extra positionals collected into a tuple), and **kwargs (extra keywords collected into a dict). The caller's arguments bind left to right, and anything unmatched spills into *args/**kwargs. Worked example:

def deploy(service, env="staging", *flags, **opts):
    print(service, env, flags, opts)

deploy("api", "prod", "--force", "--dry-run", timeout=30)

Solution: prints "api prod ('--force', '--dry-run') {'timeout': 30}". The walkthrough: service binds "api", env binds "prod" (overriding the default), the two leftover positional strings collect into flags as a tuple, and timeout=30 collects into opts as a dict. Two rules panels probe. First, defaults are evaluated once at function definition time — a mutable default like def f(x=[]) shares one list across all calls, so the idiom is def f(x=None): followed by x = x or []. Second, return ends the function immediately and a bare return (or falling off the end) yields None — code after a return never runs, which is a favorite predict-output trap. When reading a call, always map each argument to its parameter before tracing the body; most script-reading errors come from misbinding, not from misunderstanding the loop.

notes.title: Comprehensions: dense, readable data transformation
notes.body:
Comprehensions build lists, dicts, and sets in a single expression: [expression for item in iterable if condition]. They are the idiomatic way DevOps scripts filter inventories, parse ports, and reshape API responses. Worked example — filter an inventory to production web hosts:

hosts = [
    {"name": "web1", "env": "prod"},
    {"name": "web2", "env": "staging"},
    {"name": "db1",  "env": "prod"},
]
prod_webs = [h["name"] for h in hosts if h["env"] == "prod" and h["name"].startswith("web")]
print(prod_webs)

Solution: prints ['web1']. Walkthrough: web1 passes both tests (prod and name starts with "web"); web2 fails the env test; db1 fails the name test. Worked example two — a dict comprehension counting by key:

codes = [200, 500, 200, 503, 500, 200]
counts = {c: codes.count(c) for c in set(codes)}
print(counts)

Solution: prints {200: 3, 500: 2, 503: 1} in some order (set iteration order is not guaranteed — never assert an order for set-derived output). Read a comprehension inside-out: the for clause first, then the if filter, then the output expression. If a comprehension gets too clever to read at a glance, panels consider rewriting it as a plain loop a sign of maturity, not weakness.

notes.title: File I/O: context managers and line parsing
notes.body:
Real DevOps Python reads logs, inventories, and config files — always with the with statement, which closes the file even if an exception fires. Worked example — parse a simple status file where each line is "hostname,status":

with open("hosts.txt") as f:
    down = []
    for line in f:
        name, state = line.strip().split(",")
        if state == "down":
            down.append(name)
print(down)

Given hosts.txt containing "web1,up\nweb2,down\nweb3,up\n", the solution prints ['web2']. Walkthrough: strip() removes the trailing newline (without it, the last field would be "down\n" and the comparison would fail — the single most common file-parsing bug), split(",") unpacks into two names, and only web2 matches. Three professional habits: iterate the file object directly (never readlines() on a log that might be gigabytes), always strip() before splitting or comparing, and wrap parsing in try/except ValueError when the input is untrusted — a malformed line should be logged and skipped, not crash a 3 a.m. remediation script. For writing, the same with pattern applies: with open("out.txt", "w") as f: — and remember "w" truncates, so double-check the path before running.

notes.title: Strings, f-strings, and the gotchas panels love
notes.body:
String handling is where script-reading exercises separate fluent readers from guessers. F-strings embed expressions: f"{name}-{i:02d}" formats i as two digits with a leading zero. str.split(), strip(), startswith(), and join() do most parsing work. Worked example:

parts = "prod,us-east,api".split(",")
print("-".join(parts))
print(parts[1].upper())

Solution: prints "prod-us-east-api" then "US-EAST". Walkthrough: split(",") gives ['prod', 'us-east', 'api'], join glues them with dashes, and upper() returns a new string (strings are immutable — upper() never changes parts in place). Now the famous gotcha, which panels ask about directly:

def add_host(host, inventory=[]):
    inventory.append(host)
    return inventory

print(add_host("web1"))
print(add_host("web2"))

Solution: prints ['web1'] then ['web1', 'web2'] — the default list is created once at definition time and shared across calls. The fix: def add_host(host, inventory=None): then inventory = inventory if inventory is not None else []. When tracing any script, flag every mutable default, every in-place mutation of a shared object, and every string method (which always returns new) — those three checks catch the majority of predict-output traps.

cards.front: Why does b = a; b.append(4) also change a when a is a list?
cards.back: Assignment copies the reference, not the object — both names point at the same mutable list. Use a.copy() or list(a) for an independent copy.

cards.front: When does the else clause of a for loop execute?
cards.back: Only if the loop completes without hitting break. If break fires, the else is skipped.

cards.front: In def f(a, b='x', *args, **kwargs), where do extra positional and keyword arguments go?
cards.back: Extra positionals collect into args as a tuple; extra keywords collect into kwargs as a dict.

cards.front: What is wrong with def add(host, inventory=[]) ?
cards.back: The default list is created once at definition time and shared across calls — appends accumulate. Use inventory=None and create the list inside.

cards.front: What does [h['name'] for h in hosts if h['env'] == 'prod'] do?
cards.back: Builds a list of host names filtered to production — a list comprehension: for-clause, if-filter, output expression.

cards.front: Why must you strip() lines when parsing a text file?
cards.back: Lines end with '\n'; without strip(), the last field compares as 'down\n' instead of 'down' and matches fail.

cards.front: What does the with statement guarantee for file I/O?
cards.back: The file is closed automatically even if an exception is raised inside the block.

cards.front: What does f"{i:02d}" produce for i = 7?
cards.back: '07' — formats the integer as two digits with a leading zero.

cards.front: Do string methods like upper() modify the string in place?
cards.back: No — strings are immutable; upper() returns a new string and the original is unchanged.

cards.front: What is the difference between break and continue?
cards.back: break exits the loop entirely; continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one.

cards.front: In {'a': 1}, what does d.get('b', 0) return and why use it?
cards.back: Returns 0 — get() with a default avoids KeyError on missing keys, unlike d['b'].

cards.front: What does 'w' mode do in open('out.txt', 'w')?
cards.back: Opens for writing and truncates the file — existing content is destroyed, so verify the path first.

choices: Nothing — the loop never breaks so else is skipped
quiz.explain: i never equals 5, so the loop completes without break and the else clause runs, printing 'done'.

quiz.q: What is the output? a = [1, 2]; b = a; b = b + [3]; print(a)
quiz.explain: b + [3] builds a NEW list and rebinds b; a still points at the original [1, 2]. Only in-place methods like append would affect a.

quiz.q: What prints? print([p for p in [80, 443, 22] if p != 22])
quiz.explain: The comprehension keeps every port except 22, producing [80, 443].

quiz.q:
def g(svc, env='staging', **opts): print(env, opts)
What does g('api', 'prod', timeout=30) print?
quiz.explain: 'prod' overrides the default env positionally, and timeout=30 collects into opts as a dict.

quiz.q: A script reads lines 'web2,down\n' and compares fields to 'down' without strip(). What happens?
choices: The comparison fails because the field is 'down\n'
quiz.explain: The trailing newline stays on the last field, so 'down\n' != 'down' — the classic file-parsing bug.

quiz.q: What is the result of {'x': 1}['y'] versus {'x': 1}.get('y', 0)?
quiz.explain: Direct indexing raises KeyError on a missing key; get() with a default returns the default instead.

quiz.q:
What does this print? for c in [200, 200, 500]:
    if c == 200: continue
    print(c)
quiz.explain: continue skips the 200 iterations before the print; only 500 reaches print.

quiz.q: x = 'a,b,c'; what are x.split(',') and '-'.join(x.split(','))?
quiz.explain: split(',') gives the list ['a','b','c']; join glues them with dashes into 'a-b-c'.

quiz.q:
How many lines does this print, and what? name='db'
for i in range(1, 3): print(f'{name}-{i:02d}')
quiz.explain: range(1, 3) yields 1 and 2 (two iterations), and :02d zero-pads each to two digits.

drills.title: Predict the output — original script-reading drills

Predict the exact output:

print(add_host('web1'))

    print(f'{name}-{i:02d}')

Predict the exact output:

web2,down
web3,up
'

items.prompt: Is a tuple mutable or immutable? What does that imply for using one as a dict key?
items.answer: Immutable — and because immutable, tuples are hashable and can be dict keys (unlike lists).
items.explain: Immutability enables hashing; mutability forbids it.

items.prompt: What does the * in *args do at call time versus at definition time?
items.answer: At definition it collects extra positionals into a tuple; at a call site, * unpacks an iterable into separate positional arguments.
items.explain: Definition collects, call-site unpacks — the two directions of *.

items.prompt: Why is iterating a file object directly better than readlines() for logs?
items.answer: Iteration streams line by line with constant memory; readlines() loads the entire file, which can exhaust memory on gigabyte logs.
items.explain: Streaming versus whole-file load.

items.prompt: What is the difference between == and is?
items.answer: == compares values for equality; is checks whether two names reference the identical object.
items.explain: Use == for values; is is for identity (e.g. comparing with None).

items.prompt: Rewrite as a comprehension: result = []; for x in range(10): if x % 2 == 0: result.append(x * 2)
items.answer: result = [x * 2 for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]
items.explain: Output expression first, then the for clause, then the if filter.

items.prompt: A function ends without a return statement. What does calling it produce?
items.answer: None — falling off the end of a function returns None implicitly.
items.explain: Every Python call returns something; without return it is None.

items.prompt: When should you prefer a plain loop over a clever comprehension?
items.answer: When the comprehension is hard to read at a glance, has side effects, or needs complex error handling — readability wins.
items.explain: Panels reward the judgment to choose clarity over density.

handsOnLab.title: Log parser: from reading to writing scripts
handsOnLab.brief: You will write a small Python log-analysis script that parses a generated access log, counts status codes, finds the slowest endpoint, and prints a summary — then verify your output predictions by running it.
steps: Create the lab directory and file: mkdir py-reading-lab && cd py-reading-lab, then create parse_logs.py (empty for now).

Generate a sample log: write gen.py that writes 200 lines of 'METHOD /path STATUS MS' (e.g. 'GET /api/users 200 42') with random choices from a fixed seed (random.seed(7)) so output is reproducible, then run python3 gen.py to produce access.log.
In parse_logs.py, open access.log with a with statement and iterate line by line — do not use readlines().
Parse each line with strip().split() into method, path, status, ms; convert status and ms to int inside a try/except ValueError that skips malformed lines with a counter.
Count requests per status code in a dict using d.get(code, 0) + 1.
Track the slowest request: keep (ms, method, path) of the maximum seen so far.
Collect error paths: build a list of paths whose status >= 500 using a comprehension over your parsed records.
Print a summary: total lines, skipped lines, per-status counts sorted by code, slowest request, and number of error paths.
Before running, write your predicted summary numbers in predictions.txt by reasoning about the seeded generator (or compute them independently).
Run python3 parse_logs.py, diff actual versus predictions.txt, and fix any mismatch by re-tracing — not by editing the script to match.

mockTask.q: Panel shows a script with def register(host, seen=[]) that appends each host and returns seen, called three times. They ask: 'What does the third call return, and is this code production-safe?'
choices: Only the third host — each call gets a fresh list; it is safe
All three hosts accumulated — the default list is shared; it is a bug, use None default
An empty list — defaults are re-evaluated per call
It raises TypeError on the second call
mockTask.explain: Mutable defaults are created once at def time and shared, so hosts accumulate across calls — the classic gotcha. The fix is def register(host, seen=None) with seen = seen if seen is not None else [] inside.

title: Python for DevOps: APIs, Subprocess & Dependency Pinning
summary: Turn Python into an operations tool: call REST APIs safely with requests, drive system commands with subprocess, build argparse CLIs, and pin dependencies reproducibly — the scripting backbone of every DevOps workflow.
objectives: Make HTTP API calls with requests using timeouts and explicit status-code handling.
Run and capture system commands with subprocess.run without shell-injection risk.
Parse JSON and YAML configuration into Python data structures.
Build a command-line tool with argparse, exit codes, and helpful --help output.
Create virtualenvs and write pinned requirements files that make builds reproducible.

notes.title: requests: the timeout is not optional
notes.body:
Almost every DevOps script talks to an HTTP API — cloud providers, monitoring, artifact registries. The requests library makes it pleasant, but there is one rule professionals never break: always pass a timeout. Without it, a hung server hangs your script forever, and at 3 a.m. that means a remediation job that never finishes. Worked example:

import requests

resp = requests.get("https://httpbin.org/get", timeout=10)
print(resp.status_code)
print(resp.json()["url"])

Solution: prints 200, then "https://httpbin.org/get". Walkthrough: requests.get returns a Response; .status_code is the integer code; .json() parses the body. The timeout=10 means "give up after 10 seconds" — pass a tuple like timeout=(5, 30) to separate connect and read timeouts when you need finer control. Two more habits: check resp.ok or call resp.raise_for_status() instead of assuming 200, because APIs return 201, 204, 429, and 503 in normal operation; and never put secrets in URLs — use the headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"} pattern with the token from an environment variable. A script that calls an API without a timeout and without status handling is the single most common defect in take-home automation exercises.

notes.title: POSTing JSON and handling API errors
notes.body:
Reading is half the job; the other half is creating and updating resources — opening tickets, triggering pipelines, registering webhooks. requests.post with the json= parameter serializes your dict and sets the Content-Type header automatically. Worked example:

import requests

payload = {"service": "api", "env": "prod", "replicas": 3}
resp = requests.post("https://httpbin.org/post", json=payload, timeout=10)
resp.raise_for_status()
echoed = resp.json()["json"]
print(echoed["replicas"])

Solution: prints 3. Walkthrough: json=payload sends the dict as a JSON body; raise_for_status() throws an HTTPError on 4xx/5xx so failures cannot slip by silently; httpbin echoes the JSON back under the "json" key, so echoed["replicas"] is 3. The panel-relevant pattern is what surrounds the call:

try:
    resp = requests.post(url, json=payload, timeout=10)
    resp.raise_for_status()
except requests.Timeout:
    print("API timed out — will retry")
except requests.HTTPError as e:
    print("API error:", e)

Catch Timeout separately from HTTPError because the remediation differs: timeouts merit a retry with backoff, while a 400 means your payload is wrong and retrying is pointless. Always log the status code and a correlation ID — "it failed" is not a debuggable incident report.

notes.title: subprocess: running system commands safely
notes.body:
When Python must drive the system — kubectl, docker, systemctl, git — subprocess.run is the modern interface. The critical choice is shell=False (the default) with the command as a list: each list element is one argument, so a hostile filename can never become a second command. Worked example:

import subprocess

result = subprocess.run(
    ["kubectl", "get", "pods", "-n", "prod", "-o", "json"],
    capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=30, check=False,
)
print("rc:", result.returncode)
print("bytes:", len(result.stdout))

Solution: prints the real return code (0 on a healthy cluster) and the byte length of the JSON output. Walkthrough: capture_output=True grabs stdout/stderr instead of inheriting the terminal; text=True decodes to str; timeout=30 bounds the call; check=False (default) means a nonzero exit does NOT raise — you inspect result.returncode yourself. Use check=True only when any failure should abort the script. Never do subprocess.run(f"kubectl get {user_input}", shell=True) — with shell=True the string is parsed by a shell and user_input containing "; rm -rf" executes. If you truly need shell features (pipes), keep shell=True but never interpolate untrusted data, or better, chain two subprocess.run calls with pipes in Python. Prefer passing lists, always set a timeout, and log result.stderr on failure.

notes.title: Parsing JSON and YAML configuration
notes.body:
DevOps scripts constantly read config: JSON from APIs and files, YAML from Kubernetes manifests and pipeline definitions. Python's json module is stdlib; YAML needs the third-party pyyaml package (import yaml). Worked example — read a JSON service catalog and a YAML deploy config:

import json

catalog = json.loads('{"services": [{"name": "api", "port": 8080}]}')
print(catalog["services"][0]["port"])

Solution: prints 8080 — json.loads turns the JSON string into nested dicts/lists. For YAML:

import yaml

with open("deploy.yaml") as f:
    config = yaml.safe_load(f)
print(config["replicas"])

Given deploy.yaml containing "replicas: 3\nimage: api:v2\n", this prints 3. Always use yaml.safe_load, never yaml.load — the unsafe loader can construct arbitrary Python objects from hostile YAML, a real deserialization risk. Two reading habits: validate the shape after parsing (config.get("replicas") with a sensible default beats a KeyError at 3 a.m.), and when writing JSON for machines use json.dump(obj, f, indent=2, sort_keys=True) so diffs are stable and reviewable. Panels often ask you to extract one value from a nested API response by hand — practice navigating dict-in-list-in-dict without running the code.

notes.title: argparse: CLIs people can actually use
notes.body:
An automation script nobody can invoke correctly is shelfware. argparse turns a script into a real CLI with --help, types, defaults, and required flags. Worked example — the skeleton of the health-check tool you will build in the lab:

import argparse

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Check an HTTP endpoint and exit nonzero on failure.")
parser.add_argument("url", help="Endpoint to check, e.g. https://api.example.com/healthz")
parser.add_argument("--timeout", type=int, default=10, help="Seconds before giving up (default: 10)")
parser.add_argument("--expect", type=int, default=200, help="Expected HTTP status (default: 200)")
args = parser.parse_args()
print(args.url, args.timeout, args.expect)

Run as python3 healthcheck.py https://example.com --timeout 5 and it prints "https://example.com 5 200". Walkthrough: the positional url is required (argparse errors out with usage text if missing); --timeout and --expect are optional with typed, defaulted values — type=int converts and validates, rejecting "--timeout abc" with a clear error. Three professional touches: a description string (it becomes the --help header), explicit defaults shown in help text, and exiting with distinct codes (0 healthy, 1 unhealthy, 2 usage/config error) so CI pipelines and cron can branch on the result. Never parse sys.argv by hand — argparse is stdlib, tested, and expected.

notes.title: Virtualenvs and pinning: reproducible automation
notes.body:
A script that works on your laptop and breaks in CI is usually a dependency problem: different package versions. The fix has two parts. First, isolate with a virtualenv so the script's packages never fight the system Python: python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate && pip install requests. Second, pin every dependency with == in requirements.txt — the exact lesson from the M17 MR review. Worked example:

$ pip freeze > requirements.txt
$ cat requirements.txt
requests==2.32.3

That file, committed to the repo, means every install — laptop, CI, container — resolves the identical tree. Unpinned requirements (a bare requests line) resolve to whatever is newest on install day, so the code you tested is not the code you deploy. The hashes concept goes one step further: pip install --require-hashes verifies each downloaded wheel against a recorded SHA256, defeating a compromised mirror serving a trojaned package — generate them with pip hash on the downloaded files or pip-compile. Practical rules: pin runtime deps in requirements.txt, keep test tooling in requirements-test.txt, never commit the .venv directory itself, and regenerate pins deliberately (upgrade, test, re-pin) rather than letting them drift. A panel asked to review a requirements.txt expects exactly this verdict-first reasoning.

cards.front: What is the one requests rule you must never break?
cards.back: Always pass a timeout — without it a hung server hangs your script forever.

cards.front: What does resp.raise_for_status() do?
cards.back: Raises an HTTPError on 4xx/5xx responses so API failures cannot pass silently; call it (or check status) instead of assuming 200.

cards.front: Why catch requests.Timeout separately from requests.HTTPError?
cards.back: Timeouts merit a retry with backoff; a 400 means your payload is wrong and retrying is pointless — different failures need different remediation.

cards.front: Why is subprocess.run(['kubectl','get','pods']) safer than subprocess.run('kubectl get ' + user_input, shell=True)?
cards.back: With a list and shell=False each element is one argument, so hostile input cannot become a second command; shell=True lets injected input like '; rm -rf' execute.

cards.front: In subprocess.run, what do capture_output, text, timeout, and check do?
cards.back: capture_output grabs stdout/stderr; text decodes to str; timeout bounds the call; check=True raises on nonzero exit (default False — inspect returncode yourself).

cards.front: Why yaml.safe_load instead of yaml.load?
cards.back: The unsafe loader can construct arbitrary Python objects from hostile YAML — a deserialization risk. safe_load restricts to basic types.

cards.front: What does argparse give you that hand-parsing sys.argv does not?
cards.back: --help text, typed/validated options, defaults, required flags, and clear usage errors — all from the stdlib.

cards.front: What exit-code convention should a health-check CLI use?
cards.back: 0 = healthy, 1 = unhealthy, 2 = usage/config error — so CI and cron can branch on the result.

cards.front: Why pin dependencies with == in requirements.txt?
cards.back: Unpinned installs resolve to whatever is newest on install day, so the tested artifact differs from the deployed one; pins make every install identical.

cards.front: What does pip install --require-hashes add beyond == pins?
cards.back: It verifies each downloaded wheel against a recorded SHA256, defeating a compromised mirror serving a trojaned package.

cards.front: Should the .venv directory be committed to git?
cards.back: No — commit requirements.txt (the recipe), never the environment itself.

cards.front: Where does pytest belong: requirements.txt or requirements-test.txt?
cards.back: requirements-test.txt — test tooling does not belong in the production install (leaner images, smaller attack surface).

quiz.q: A script calls requests.get(url) with no timeout. What is the operational risk?
choices: A hung server hangs the script indefinitely
quiz.explain: Without a timeout there is no bound on how long the call can block — a hung server means a hung automation job.

quiz.q: What does timeout=(5, 30) mean in requests?
choices: 5 seconds connect timeout, 30 seconds read timeout
30 seconds connect timeout, 5 seconds read timeout
quiz.explain: The tuple form separates the connect timeout from the read timeout for finer control.

quiz.q: Which subprocess call is safe against shell injection with untrusted filename input?
quiz.explain: A list with shell=False passes filename as a single argument; every shell=True option lets injected metacharacters execute.

quiz.q: subprocess.run(['kubectl','get','pods'], capture_output=True, text=True) — what do the flags do?
choices: They stream output live to the terminal
They capture stdout/stderr and decode to str instead of bytes
They run the command as text, not binary
quiz.explain: capture_output grabs the streams; text=True decodes bytes to str so you can parse directly.

quiz.q: Why must you use yaml.safe_load on untrusted YAML?
choices: The unsafe loader can construct arbitrary Python objects — a deserialization attack
Untrusted YAML cannot be parsed otherwise
quiz.explain: yaml.load can instantiate arbitrary objects from hostile input; safe_load restricts parsing to basic types.

quiz.q: In argparse, what does parser.add_argument('--timeout', type=int, default=10) provide?
choices: An optional flag, converted to int, defaulting to 10, rejected with a clear error if not numeric
quiz.explain: type=int validates and converts; default supplies the fallback; invalid input produces a clean usage error.

quiz.q: A requirements.txt lists bare 'requests' with no version. What breaks?
choices: Reproducibility: installs on different days may resolve different versions
quiz.explain: Unpinned requirements float with the newest release, so tested code and deployed code can differ.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of pip freeze > requirements.txt?
choices: To record the exact installed versions so others can reproduce the environment
quiz.explain: freeze snapshots the working set's exact versions into the pin file you commit.

quiz.q: An API returns 429. Your script called raise_for_status() inside try/except HTTPError. What should the handler do?
choices: Retry immediately in a tight loop
Back off and retry, honoring any Retry-After guidance — 429 means rate-limited
quiz.explain: 429 signals rate limiting; the correct remediation is backoff-and-retry, not hammering the API.

items.prompt: Write the requests call to GET https://api.example.com/healthz with a 10-second timeout, raising on HTTP errors.
items.answer: resp = requests.get('https://api.example.com/healthz', timeout=10); resp.raise_for_status()
items.explain: Timeout bounds the call; raise_for_status converts 4xx/5xx into exceptions instead of silent failures.

items.prompt: How do you POST the dict {'replicas': 3} as JSON and read back the echoed value?
items.answer: resp = requests.post(url, json={'replicas': 3}, timeout=10); resp.raise_for_status(); value = resp.json()['replicas']
items.explain: json= serializes and sets Content-Type; .json() parses the response body back into Python.

items.prompt: Where should an API token live, and how does it reach the request?
items.answer: In an environment variable (never hardcoded or in URLs); passed via headers={'Authorization': f'Bearer {token}'}.
items.explain: Env vars keep secrets out of code and URLs keep them out of logs.

items.prompt: Run 'kubectl get pods -n prod -o json' from Python, capturing output as text with a 30s timeout. Write the call.
items.answer: subprocess.run(['kubectl','get','pods','-n','prod','-o','json'], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=30)
items.explain: List form with shell=False (no injection), capture_output+text for parseable str, timeout to bound the call.

items.prompt: The command above returns exit code 1. How do you detect it, and when would check=True be appropriate?
items.answer: Inspect result.returncode (check defaults False); use check=True when any failure should abort the script via CalledProcessError.
items.explain: Default gives you control to branch on the code; check=True is the fail-fast option.

items.prompt: Parse the JSON string '{"port": 8080}' and print the port. Write the code.
items.answer: import json; print(json.loads('{"port": 8080}')['port'])
items.explain: json.loads converts the JSON string to a dict; index the key.

items.prompt: A script reads deploy.yaml from an untrusted source. Which loader and why?
items.answer: yaml.safe_load — the default yaml.load can construct arbitrary Python objects, a deserialization risk on hostile input.
items.explain: safe_load restricts to basic types.

items.prompt: Define an argparse positional 'url' and optional '--timeout' (int, default 10). Write the snippet.
items.answer: p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description='...'); p.add_argument('url'); p.add_argument('--timeout', type=int, default=10); args = p.parse_args()
items.explain: Positional is required by default; the option is typed, defaulted, and self-documenting in --help.

items.prompt: Your CLI is used by CI. Which exit codes do you use for healthy, unhealthy, and bad usage?
items.answer: 0 healthy, 1 unhealthy, 2 usage/config error.
items.explain: Distinct codes let pipelines and cron branch on the outcome.

items.prompt: Create and activate a virtualenv, then install requests into it. Give the commands.
items.answer: python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate && pip install requests
items.explain: Isolates the script's packages from the system Python.

items.prompt: Generate a pinned requirements file from the active venv. Give the command and explain what it records.
items.answer: pip freeze > requirements.txt — records exact installed versions so every environment installs identically.
items.explain: The pin file is the reproducibility contract you commit.

items.prompt: An MR adds requirements.txt with 'requests' unpinned. Verdict and fix?
items.answer: Request changes: pin as requests==<verified-version> so builds are reproducible.
items.explain: The M17 review rule applied: verdict first, then the fix.

items.prompt: What does --require-hashes protect against that == pins do not?
items.answer: A compromised mirror serving a trojaned wheel with the right version number — hashes verify the actual bytes.
items.explain: Pins name the version; hashes verify the content.

items.prompt: Should pytest go in requirements.txt for a production container image? Why?
items.answer: No — test tooling belongs in requirements-test.txt; shipping it bloats the image and widens the attack surface.
items.explain: Separation of runtime and test dependency sets.

handsOnLab.title: Build a CLI health-check tool
handsOnLab.brief: You will build healthcheck.py — an argparse CLI that GETs a URL with a timeout, compares the status to an expected code, exits 0/1/2 appropriately, and ships with a pinned requirements.txt generated from a virtualenv.
steps: Set up: mkdir healthcheck-lab && cd healthcheck-lab && python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate && pip install requests.
Write healthcheck.py with argparse: positional 'url', --timeout (int, default 10), --expect (int, default 200), and a --retries (int, default 0) flag.

title: Concurrency, the GIL & Health-Probe-Friendly Services
summary: Understand threads, processes, and async in Python, what the GIL really limits, and why single-threaded services fail Kubernetes readiness probes under load — then design probe-friendly services with separate /healthz endpoints and timeouts everywhere.
objectives: Compare threads, processes, and async I/O and choose the right model for a workload.
Explain the GIL's effect on CPU-bound versus I/O-bound Python code.
Diagnose why a single-threaded Python service fails readiness probes under load.
Design separate liveness and readiness endpoints with correct semantics.
Apply timeouts and non-blocking patterns so slow dependencies cannot cascade.

notes.title: Threads, processes, async: three kinds of concurrency
The GIL: what it actually limits
notes.body: CPython's Global Interpreter Lock allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. This is the single most misunderstood fact in Python interviews, so be precise: the GIL limits CPU-bound threading, not I/O-bound threading. During I/O — network reads, disk waits, time.sleep — a thread releases the GIL, so other threads run. During pure Python computation, they take turns and you gain no speedup (and may lose a little to switching overhead). Worked example — two workloads, two outcomes. Workload A: four threads each downloading a file. Result: roughly 4x faster than sequential, because the threads spend their time waiting on the network with the GIL released. Workload B: four threads each hashing data in a tight Python loop. Result: no faster than sequential — the GIL serializes the bytecode execution. The fixes for B are multiprocessing (each process has its own GIL and its own core) or pushing the hot loop into C (numpy, hashlib releases the GIL internally). For DevOps services — which are overwhelmingly I/O-bound, waiting on APIs, databases, and queues — threads and async are usually the right answer, and "the GIL makes Python slow" is not a valid objection to them. Know the boundary cold: GIL bites CPU-bound threads; it does not bite I/O-bound ones.

notes.title: Panel question: why single-threaded Python fails readiness probes under load
notes.body: This is a real panel question: a single-threaded Python service passes health checks at low traffic, then starts failing readiness probes under load — while the equivalent Java service survives. Here is the mechanism. A single-threaded server handles one request at a time. Each request does slow work — a database query, a downstream API call — taking, say, 800ms. At low traffic that is fine. Under load, requests queue behind the one being served. The readiness probe is just another HTTP request to /healthz, and it joins the same queue. If the probe cannot get a response within its timeout, the kubelet marks the pod unready and pulls it out of the service — even though the app is technically alive and working through its queue. Traffic shifts to the remaining pods, which now take more load, queue longer, and fail their probes too: a cascading failure from a healthy-but-slow service. The Java comparison: a typical Java server uses a thread pool or non-blocking I/O, so the probe request gets a thread immediately even while others are busy. The Python fix is the same idea — serve probes concurrently with work (threads, async, or a separate probe server), keep the probe endpoint trivially cheap, and set aggressive timeouts on downstream calls so no single request can hold the server for seconds.

notes.title: Separate /healthz endpoints: liveness vs readiness vs startup
Timeouts everywhere: stop slow dependencies from cascading
Async patterns: non-blocking services without thread pools
notes.body:
asyncio lets one thread juggle thousands of connections by suspending tasks at await points instead of blocking. The mental model: async def functions return coroutines; await yields control while waiting; the event loop resumes whichever task is ready. Worked example — concurrent health checks with asyncio.gather:

import asyncio

async def check(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)  # stands in for an I/O wait
    return f"{name} ok"

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(check("db"), check("cache"))
    print(results)

asyncio.run(main())

Solution: prints ['db ok', 'cache ok'] after about one second — both sleeps overlap on the single thread, and gather preserves result order. Two rules that prevent the classic async defects. One: never call blocking code (time.sleep, requests.get, heavy computation) inside async functions without await — it freezes the entire event loop, and every connection stalls; offload blocking calls with asyncio.to_thread or loop.run_in_executor. Two: async only helps I/O-bound work; CPU-bound coroutines still serialize on the one thread. For probe-friendly services, the async payoff is direct: the /healthz handler is a tiny coroutine that answers between awaits of the slow work, so probes stay fast under load without managing a thread pool. That is the modern answer to the panel's single-threaded-Python question.

cards.front: Threads vs processes vs async — when is each the right choice?
cards.back: Threads: I/O-bound work, shared memory, cheap. Processes: CPU-bound work needing true parallelism (own GIL each). Async: massive I/O connection counts on one thread, switching at await points.

cards.front: What does the GIL limit, precisely?
cards.back: Only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time in CPython — so CPU-bound threads gain no speedup, while I/O-bound threads still win because the GIL is released during I/O waits.

cards.front: Why does a single-threaded Python service fail readiness probes under load?
cards.back: One request at a time means probe requests queue behind slow work; when /healthz cannot answer within its timeout, the kubelet marks the pod unready — cascading as traffic shifts to fewer pods.

cards.front: Liveness vs readiness probe: what happens when each fails?
cards.back: Liveness failure restarts the container; readiness failure only removes the pod from service traffic without restarting.

cards.front: What should a liveness endpoint do, and what should it NOT do?
cards.back: Do: answer trivially with no I/O. Do NOT: deep-check dependencies — a dead database is not a dead container, and restarting on a DB blip turns a pause into an outage.

cards.front: What is a startup probe for?
cards.back: It gates liveness/readiness for slow-starting containers so a long warmup does not trigger restarts or premature traffic.

cards.front: Name three timeout layers a production service needs.
cards.back: Client timeouts on every outbound call; server timeouts bounding request handlers; probe timeoutSeconds shorter than the probe period — plus connection-pool limits.

cards.front: Why do timeouts matter more than retries?
cards.back: Timeouts convert hangs into errors; errors are retryable, alertable, and survivable, while hangs silently consume workers until the service collapses.

cards.front: What freezes an asyncio event loop, and how do you avoid it?
cards.back: Blocking calls (time.sleep, requests.get, CPU work) with no await freeze every connection; offload them with asyncio.to_thread or run_in_executor.

cards.front: Does asyncio help CPU-bound work?
cards.back: No — coroutines still share one thread, so CPU-bound work serializes; use multiprocessing for CPU-bound parallelism.

cards.front: In the gather example, why do two 1-second sleeps finish in ~1 second total?
cards.back: await suspends each coroutine during its sleep so both waits overlap on the single thread; gather preserves result order.

cards.front: A pod is running but gets restarted repeatedly. Which probe is the suspect, and what do you check?
cards.back: The liveness probe — check whether it does expensive dependency checks (it should be trivially cheap) and whether timeoutSeconds/periodSeconds fit the app's real response time.

quiz.q: Four threads each download a file (I/O-bound) under CPython. Expected speedup vs sequential?
choices: No speedup — the GIL serializes everything
Roughly 4x faster, since the GIL is released during I/O waits
Slower, because threads cannot do I/O
quiz.explain: Threads release the GIL while waiting on I/O, so I/O-bound threaded work overlaps and speeds up; the GIL only serializes CPU-bound bytecode.

quiz.q: Four threads each hash data in a tight Python loop. Expected result?
choices: No speedup — the GIL serializes the bytecode
quiz.explain: CPU-bound Python threads take turns on the GIL; use multiprocessing (own GIL per process) for CPU-bound parallelism.

quiz.q: Panel: single-threaded Python service fails readiness probes under load but Java survives. Root cause?
choices: Probe requests queue behind slow requests on the single thread and time out; Java's thread pool/NIO serves probes concurrently
Kubernetes probes do not support Python
The GIL blocks all network I/O
quiz.explain: One-at-a-time serving means /healthz waits in the same queue as work requests; concurrent serving (threads/async) lets probes answer immediately.

quiz.q: The liveness probe fails. What does the kubelet do?
choices: Removes the pod from service endpoints only
quiz.explain: Liveness = 'is it dead?' → restart. Readiness = 'should it get traffic?' → remove from endpoints without restarting.

quiz.q: Your liveness endpoint pings the database with a 30s timeout. What is wrong?
choices: A DB blip will restart every pod instead of just pausing traffic; liveness must be trivially cheap
quiz.explain: Deep dependency checks belong in readiness. Wiring them as liveness turns a downstream blip into mass restarts.

quiz.q: An outbound API call has no timeout and the downstream hangs. What follows?
choices: Handlers pile up waiting, workers exhaust, probes time out — a cascading failure
Only that one request is slow
quiz.explain: One hung dependency without a timeout consumes workers until readiness fails and traffic cascades onto fewer pods.

quiz.q: Inside an async handler you call requests.get() (blocking). What happens?
choices: It runs concurrently like everything else
It freezes the entire event loop — all connections stall until it returns
It raises an async error immediately
quiz.explain: Blocking calls with no await hold the single thread; offload with asyncio.to_thread or run_in_executor.

quiz.q: What does await asyncio.gather(check('db'), check('cache')) guarantee about results?
choices: Both checks overlap in time and results come back in the gather() argument order
quiz.explain: gather runs the coroutines concurrently and returns results ordered by the argument list.

quiz.q: Which fix addresses 'service knocked over under load, failing health checks'?
choices: Serve probes concurrently (threads/async), keep /healthz trivially cheap, and set aggressive downstream timeouts
Run a single thread to reduce contention
quiz.explain: Concurrent probe serving plus cheap health endpoints plus timeouts is the cloud-native answer; masking the probe only hides the collapse.

items.prompt: Is the GIL a problem for a thread pool making 50 concurrent API calls? Why?
items.answer: No — the threads spend their time waiting on I/O with the GIL released, so they overlap and speed up.
items.explain: GIL bites CPU-bound threads, not I/O-bound ones.

items.prompt: Is the GIL a problem for threads computing checksums in pure Python? What is the fix?
items.answer: Yes — bytecode execution serializes with no speedup. Fix: multiprocessing (own GIL per process) or push the loop into C.
items.explain: CPU-bound parallelism needs processes, not threads.

items.prompt: Panel: 'Your single-threaded Python API fails readiness under load. Walk me through it.'
items.answer: One request at a time; slow requests queue; the /healthz probe joins the queue and times out; kubelet marks unready; traffic shifts to fewer pods and they cascade too.
items.explain: The full causal chain: queueing → probe timeout → unready → cascade.

items.prompt: Why does the equivalent Java service typically survive the same load?
items.answer: Thread pools or non-blocking I/O serve the probe request concurrently with slow work, so /healthz answers immediately.
items.explain: Concurrent probe serving is the difference, not language speed.

items.prompt: Give three concrete fixes for the Python service.
items.answer: Serve with threads/async so probes answer concurrently; make /healthz trivially cheap with no dependency I/O; set aggressive timeouts on downstream calls.
items.explain: Concurrency + cheap probes + timeouts — the complete answer.

items.prompt: A pod restarts in a loop during a database outage. Which probe is misconfigured and how?
items.answer: Liveness is doing deep dependency checks; move them to readiness so the outage pauses traffic instead of restarting pods.
items.explain: Liveness must be cheap; dependency checks are readiness semantics.

items.prompt: When is a startup probe the right tool?
items.answer: For slow-starting containers, to delay liveness/readiness evaluation during warmup so they do not fire prematurely.
items.explain: Startup gates the other probes during initialization.

items.prompt: Predict the output and timing: asyncio.gather(check('db'), check('cache')) where each awaits asyncio.sleep(1).
items.answer: Prints ['db ok', 'cache ok'] after ~1 second — the sleeps overlap and gather preserves argument order.
items.explain: Concurrent waits on one thread; ordered results.

items.prompt: You need 2,000 concurrent outbound connections. Threads or async — and why?
items.answer: Async — thousands of threads carry heavy memory/scheduling overhead; async tasks are cheap coroutines on one thread.
items.explain: Connection-count scale favors async's low per-task cost.

items.prompt: Name the defect: async def handler(): data = requests.get(url); return data.json()
items.answer: Blocking requests.get with no await freezes the event loop; use an async client or asyncio.to_thread.
items.explain: The classic async defect — one blocking call stalls all connections.

items.prompt: Does converting CPU-bound work to async speed it up?
items.answer: No — coroutines share one thread and CPU work does not await; use multiprocessing.
items.explain: Async helps I/O-bound concurrency only.

items.prompt: List the three timeout layers for a production service.
items.answer: Client timeouts on every outbound call; server timeouts bounding handlers; probe timeoutSeconds shorter than the period — plus pool limits.
items.explain: Defense in depth against hangs at every layer.

items.prompt: Your readiness check pings the DB. What timeout and failure behavior?
items.answer: Short timeout (e.g. 2s); on timeout return not-ready (503) so traffic pauses instead of queueing.
items.explain: Fast failure at the probe keeps the failure local.

items.prompt: Summarize in one sentence why timeouts beat retries as the first defense.
items.answer: Timeouts convert hangs into errors, and errors are retryable, alertable, and survivable — hangs are none of those.
items.explain: The panel-ready one-liner.
