title: Go Essentials for Tooling
summary: Learn enough Go to build real operations tools: syntax, error handling, modules, and cross-compilation — and understand why so much cloud-native tooling (Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform) ships as single Go binaries.
objectives: Explain why Go fits operations tooling: single static binaries, fast startup, strong stdlib.
Write basic Go programs using packages, functions, slices, and maps.
Handle errors the Go way with explicit multiple return values.
Initialize a module and build a binary with the go toolchain.
Cross-compile one codebase for Linux, Windows, and macOS targets.

notes.title: Why Go owns the ops-tooling niche
notes.body:
A remarkable share of cloud-native tooling — Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, Prometheus — is written in Go, and the reasons are practical, not fashionable. First, Go compiles to a single statically linked binary: you ship one file with no runtime to install, no virtualenv to activate, no dependency tree to resolve on the target machine. Second, startup is instant — a Go CLI answers in milliseconds, while a JVM or Python-based tool pays interpreter or VM warmup on every invocation, which matters when the tool runs inside tight automation loops. Third, the standard library covers the ops basics out of the box: HTTP clients and servers, JSON, flags, templating, and cryptography, so small tools need zero third-party packages. Fourth, cross-compilation is a one-line environment change (next notes), so one codebase ships for every platform your fleet runs. Worked example of the payoff — the entire release process for the port-checker you will build in the lab is:

$ go build -o portcheck .

One command, one binary, runs anywhere. The trade-off to name honestly: Go is more verbose than Python for quick scripts, and its type system demands more upfront design. For a 20-line glue script, Python wins; for a tool you will distribute, run a million times, and maintain for years, Go's binary is the professional choice.

notes.title: First Go program: packages, funcs, and types
notes.body:
Every Go program starts with package main and func main — the entry point the toolchain looks for. Variables declared with := get their type inferred; the fmt package handles formatted I/O. Worked example:

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    name := "api"
    port := 8080
    healthy := true
    fmt.Printf("%s listening on %d (healthy=%t)\n", name, port, healthy)
}

Solution: prints "api listening on 8080 (healthy=true)". Walkthrough: := declares and infers (string, int, bool); Printf verbs %s/%d/%t format each type; \n is the newline. Key type facts: Go is statically typed — name cannot later hold an int, and the compiler rejects it. Integers have explicit sizes (int, int64); strings are immutable UTF-8 byte sequences; bool is a real type, not an int alias. Unused variables and imports are compile errors, not warnings — the compiler enforces hygiene. Run it without building via go run main.go. Two habits from day one: gofmt your code (go fmt ./...) so formatting debates never happen, and read compiler errors literally — Go's errors point at the exact line and are unusually actionable compared to template-heavy languages.

notes.title: Slices, maps, and control flow
Error handling: explicit, not exceptional
Modules and the build: go mod init to go build
notes.body:
Go modules are the dependency and build story: a go.mod file names your module and pins every dependency's version, giving reproducible builds like a requirements.txt with teeth. Worked example — from zero to binary:

$ mkdir portcheck && cd portcheck
$ go mod init example.com/portcheck
go: creating new go.mod: module example.com/portcheck
$ go run .
$ go build -o portcheck .
$ ./portcheck --help

Walkthrough: go mod init creates go.mod (module path plus go version); go run compiles to a temp binary and executes it — the fast edit loop; go build -o portcheck . produces the real distributable binary in the current directory. Dependencies enter via go get (e.g. go get github.com/spf13/cobra) and land pinned in go.mod with hashes in go.sum — commit both files, exactly like committing a pinned requirements.txt. go vet ./... runs the built-in static analyzer (catches Printf verb mismatches and suspicious constructs) and belongs in every CI pipeline; gofmt -l . lists unformatted files. No Makefile is needed for small tools — the toolchain is the build system. The mental model: go.mod is the contract, go.sum is the integrity proof, and the single binary is the artifact you ship to every machine in the fleet.

notes.title: Cross-compilation and a real CLI: the port checker
notes.body:
Cross-compilation is Go's superpower for ops: set GOOS and GOARCH and the same source builds for another platform — no container, no VM, no cross toolchain to install. Worked example:

$ GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build -o portcheck-linux .
$ GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build -o portcheck.exe .
$ GOOS=darwin GOARCH=arm64 go build -o portcheck-mac .
$ file portcheck-linux
portcheck-linux: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, statically linked

One codebase, three fleet-ready binaries. And here is the CLI itself, using only the stdlib flag package — the tool you will build in the lab:

package main

import (
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "net"
    "os"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    host := flag.String("host", "localhost", "host to check")
    port := flag.Int("port", 80, "port to check")
    timeout := flag.Duration("timeout", 5*time.Second, "dial timeout")
    flag.Parse()

    addr := fmt.Sprintf("%s:%d", *host, *port)
    conn, err := net.DialTimeout("tcp", addr, *timeout)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Println("CLOSED:", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    conn.Close()
    fmt.Println("OPEN:", addr)
}

Run ./portcheck -host db.internal -port 5432 -timeout 3s. Flags are pointers (*host dereferences); DialTimeout bounds the dial so a dead host fails in 3 seconds, not 2 minutes; exit 1 on closed keeps the CI contract. This is production-shaped Go: stdlib only, explicit errors, timeouts everywhere.

cards.front: Why is Go popular for operations tooling?
cards.back: Single statically linked binary (nothing to install), instant startup, strong stdlib (HTTP, JSON, flags), and trivial cross-compilation.

cards.front: What do 'package main' and 'func main' signify?
cards.back: They mark the program's entry point — the toolchain builds an executable starting at func main in package main.

cards.front: What does := do, and what is Go's stance on unused variables?
cards.back: := declares a variable with inferred type; unused variables or imports are compile errors, not warnings.

cards.front: How do you detect a missing key in a Go map?
cards.back: Use the two-value form: v, ok := m[key] — ok is false when absent. Single-value indexing returns the zero value silently.

cards.front: How does Go signal errors, and what is the calling convention?
cards.back: No exceptions — functions return error as (usually) the last value; callers check if err != nil before using the result.

cards.front: What does fmt.Errorf("dial %s: %w", addr, err) accomplish?
cards.back: Wraps the root error with context while %w preserves unwrapping, so callers can still inspect the original cause.

cards.front: What are go.mod and go.sum, and should you commit them?
cards.back: go.mod names the module and pins dependency versions; go.sum holds integrity hashes — commit both for reproducible builds.

cards.front: What is the difference between go run and go build?
cards.back: go run compiles to a temp binary and executes it (fast edit loop); go build produces the distributable binary file.

cards.front: Give the commands to cross-compile for Windows amd64 and macOS arm64.
cards.back: GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build -o app.exe . and GOOS=darwin GOARCH=arm64 go build -o app-mac .

cards.front: In the flag package, why do you write *host instead of host?
cards.back: flag.String returns a *string pointer; you dereference it to get the value.

cards.front: Why does the port checker use net.DialTimeout instead of net.Dial?
cards.back: DialTimeout bounds the dial so a dead host fails fast (e.g. 3s) instead of hanging for minutes — the timeouts-everywhere rule.

cards.front: What CI checks belong on every Go repo?
cards.back: gofmt for formatting, go vet ./... for static analysis, and building (plus tests) on every change.

quiz.q: What is the primary distribution advantage of a Go tool over a Python script?
choices: Go compiles to a single static binary with no runtime to install on targets
Go does not need a compiler
quiz.explain: One static binary ships and runs anywhere — no interpreter, virtualenv, or dependency install on the target machine.

quiz.q: What does this print? name := "api"; port := 8080; fmt.Printf("%s:%d", name, port)
quiz.explain: := infers string and int; %s formats the string, %d the integer.

quiz.q: status := map[string]string{"a": "up"}; fmt.Println(status["b"]). What prints and why?
choices: An empty string — missing keys return the zero value
quiz.explain: Single-value map indexing on a missing key yields the zero value silently; use v, ok := status["b"] to detect absence.

quiz.q: A function returns (int, error). What is the idiomatic handling?
choices: Use the int first, check err later
if err != nil { handle it } before using the int
Ignore err if the int looks right
quiz.explain: Go has no exceptions; you must check err != nil explicitly before trusting the other return value.

quiz.q: What does GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build -o app.exe . do?
choices: Builds for the current machine only
Cross-compiles the package for 64-bit Windows without needing a Windows machine
quiz.explain: GOOS/GOARCH retarget the compiler — one codebase builds for any supported platform from anywhere.

quiz.q: Why does go vet ./... belong in CI?
choices: It runs static analysis catching bugs like Printf verb mismatches
quiz.explain: go vet is the built-in analyzer that flags suspicious constructs before they ship.

quiz.q: In flag.Duration("timeout", 5*time.Second, ...), what does the user pass and get?
choices: -timeout must be an integer of nanoseconds
Durations are not supported by flag
quiz.explain: flag.Duration parses Go duration strings like 3s or 500ms into a time.Duration value.

quiz.q: Your CLI fails to connect. Which exit behavior keeps the automation contract?
choices: Print to stderr and os.Exit(1) so callers detect failure
Panic with a stack trace always
quiz.explain: Nonzero exit codes are how CI/cron detect tool failure — same contract as the M19 Python CLI.

quiz.q: Should you commit go.sum? Why?
choices: Yes — it holds integrity hashes proving dependencies are untampered
It is generated at release time only

title: Docker: Images, Layers & the Dockerfile
summary: Learn what container images really are — stacked read-only layers plus a thin writable top — and write Dockerfiles with correct FROM, RUN, COPY, CMD, and ENTRYPOINT instructions ordered for maximum layer-cache reuse.
objectives: Distinguish images (immutable templates) from containers (running instances).
Explain what RUN does: each invocation creates a new image layer.
Write a Dockerfile using FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, ADD, EXPOSE, CMD, and ENTRYPOINT correctly.
Choose between CMD and ENTRYPOINT, and between exec form and shell form.
Order Dockerfile instructions to maximize layer-cache hits and speed up rebuilds.

notes.title: Image vs container: template vs running instance
notes.body:
An image is an immutable template: a stack of read-only filesystem layers plus metadata (which command to run, which ports to expose, which environment variables to set). A container is a running instance of an image — the same layers plus a thin writable layer on top and an isolated process namespace. The analogy panels accept: the image is the class, the container is the object. Worked example:

$ docker images
REPOSITORY   TAG     IMAGE ID       SIZE
healthcheck  v1      a91c3e27f104   148MB
$ docker run -d --name hc1 healthcheck:v1
$ docker run -d --name hc2 healthcheck:v1

Both containers share the identical read-only image layers on disk — starting hc2 costs almost nothing extra because only its thin writable layer is new. Delete a container and its writable layer vanishes; the image is untouched. This is why images are the unit of distribution (pushed to registries, scanned for vulnerabilities, promoted through environments) while containers are the unit of execution (started, stopped, replaced). A direct consequence: never store data you need to keep inside a container's writable layer — it dies with the container. Persistent data belongs in volumes (M24). And "it works on my machine" dies here too: the image carries the OS libraries, the language runtime, and the pinned dependencies, so the artifact that passed CI is byte-identical to the one running in production.

notes.title: FROM and WORKDIR: the foundation of every Dockerfile
notes.body:
FROM sets the base image — the starting layer stack your image builds on — and every Dockerfile begins with it. Choose the base deliberately: python:3.12-slim for Python apps (small, Debian-based), or a fuller variant only if you need compilation toolchains. Pin the tag (python:3.12-slim, not python:latest) for the same reproducibility reason you pin pip packages: latest floats, and a rebuild next month may pull a different base. WORKDIR sets the working directory for all following instructions — and creates it if missing. Worked example:

FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app

Every subsequent RUN, COPY, and CMD now executes relative to /app, and the directory exists in the image. Without WORKDIR, files scatter across / and COPY destinations become ambiguous — a common beginner defect. Two professional rules: prefer official images (the library/ namespace on Docker Hub) because they are maintained, scanned, and documented; and treat the base image as a dependency to be updated deliberately — schedule base-image refreshes, test, and re-pin, rather than letting a floating tag change your runtime underneath you. The base you choose determines your image's OS libraries, security patch level, and starting size, so it is an architecture decision, not a formality.

notes.title: What RUN really does: one instruction, one layer
notes.body:
This is the panel question, so learn it precisely: each RUN instruction executes a command in a temporary container based on the previous layer, then commits the resulting filesystem diff as a brand-new read-only layer. The Dockerfile is a recipe for stacking layers. Worked example:

FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir requests==2.32.3
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

Then inspect:

$ docker build -t demo:v1 .
$ docker history demo:v1

The history output shows one row per layer: the base image's layers, then a layer for the pip install, then a layer for the apt-get line — each with its size. Solution insight: docker history is the proof — count the rows and they match your RUN count (plus base). Two consequences follow. First, layers are immutable and content-addressed: identical instruction + identical parent layer = identical layer, which is what makes the build cache work. Second, everything a RUN downloads or creates lives in its layer forever (the whiteout lesson in M23) — which is why the apt-get example chains update, install, and cleanup in a SINGLE RUN: split across three RUNs, the package lists would persist in an intermediate layer even after the rm. Combine related operations in one RUN, joined with && so a failure aborts the whole step.

notes.title: COPY vs ADD: prefer the obvious one
notes.body:
COPY and ADD both place files into the image, but they differ in exactly two ways — and the guidance is simple: use COPY unless you specifically need ADD's extras. COPY takes files from the build context (the directory you build from) and places them at the destination: COPY requirements.txt . copies one file; COPY . . copies the whole context. ADD does the same plus two magic behaviors: it auto-extracts local tar archives, and it can fetch remote URLs. Worked example of the preferred pattern:

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .

This two-step COPY is deliberate layer-cache strategy (next note): dependencies install in their own layer, so editing app code later does not re-run pip. The ADD trap: ADD https://example.com/tool.tar.gz /tmp/ fetches at build time with no checksum verification and no cache invalidation control — the layer cache cannot know the remote changed, so rebuilds silently reuse stale bytes. Professionals fetch remote artifacts with RUN curl plus a checksum check instead, keeping every input explicit and verifiable. Rule: COPY for files, RUN curl for downloads, ADD almost never. One more sharp edge: COPY follows .dockerignore (M23) — without it, your .git directory and local virtualenv ride into the image, bloating it and possibly leaking secrets.

notes.title: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT: defaults vs the fixed command
notes.body:
CMD and ENTRYPOINT together define what runs when the container starts, and panels probe the difference relentlessly. ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable — it always runs. CMD provides the default arguments — appended to the entrypoint, and overridden by arguments on docker run. Worked example:

ENTRYPOINT ["python", "app.py"]
CMD ["--port", "8080"]

docker run myimage runs python app.py --port 8080; docker run myimage --port 9090 runs python app.py --port 9090 — the CMD defaults were replaced. If you instead wrote only CMD ["python", "app.py", "--port", "8080"], then docker run myimage /bin/sh would drop your app entirely and run a shell — CMD is fully replaceable, ENTRYPOINT is not. The second axis is form: the exec form ["python", "app.py"] runs the binary directly as PID 1, while the shell form CMD python app.py wraps it as /bin/sh -c "python app.py". The shell wrapper breaks signal handling — docker stop sends SIGTERM to the shell, not your app, so graceful shutdown fails and stops hang until the kill timeout. Professional default: exec-form ENTRYPOINT for the fixed command, exec-form CMD for overridable defaults, shell form never in production images. Verify with docker inspect: Entrypoint and Cmd are separate fields in the image config.

notes.title: EXPOSE and layer-cache ordering: fast rebuilds by design
notes.body:
EXPOSE documents which port the container listens on (EXPOSE 8080) — it is metadata, not a firewall rule: the port is only reachable from outside via docker run -p. Its real value is documentation and tooling: orchestrators and docker run -P read it. The performance topic is layer-cache ordering. Docker caches each layer and reuses it when the instruction and its inputs are unchanged; the first changed instruction invalidates that layer and every layer after it. Worked example — the wrong order:

COPY . .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

Every code edit changes the COPY layer, invalidating the pip layer below it — a full dependency reinstall on each build. The right order:

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .

requirements.txt changes rarely, so the expensive pip layer stays cached across dozens of code edits; only the final cheap COPY re-runs. Solution check: build twice with no changes and watch docker build report "CACHED" for every step; then touch app.py, rebuild, and confirm only the last COPY re-ran. Generalize the principle: order instructions from least-frequently-changed to most-frequently-changed — base image, system packages, language dependencies, then application code. A Dockerfile ordered this way turns a 4-minute rebuild into a 10-second one, which compounds across every CI run, every developer, every day.

cards.front: What is the difference between an image and a container?
cards.back: An image is the immutable template (read-only layers + metadata); a container is a running instance — the image layers plus a thin writable layer and an isolated process.

cards.front: Panel: what does RUN do in a Dockerfile?
cards.back: Each RUN executes in a temp container from the previous layer and commits the filesystem diff as a new read-only layer — one RUN, one layer.

cards.front: How do you prove how many layers an image has?
cards.back: docker history <image> — one row per layer, matching your RUN/COPY/FROM count plus base layers.

cards.front: Why chain apt-get update, install, and cleanup in a single RUN?
cards.back: Layers are immutable — split across RUNs, the package lists persist in an intermediate layer even after a later rm; one RUN keeps them out of the final image.

cards.front: COPY vs ADD — which do you prefer and why?
cards.back: COPY for files. ADD's extras (auto-extract, remote URLs) hide behavior; fetch remotes with RUN curl + checksum instead.

cards.front: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?
cards.back: ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable that always runs; CMD supplies default arguments appended to it, fully overridden by docker run arguments.

cards.front: Exec form vs shell form — which for production, and why?
cards.back: Exec form (["python","app.py"]) — it runs the binary directly as PID 1. Shell form wraps in /bin/sh -c, breaking signal handling so docker stop hangs.

cards.front: Does EXPOSE publish a port to the host?
cards.back: No — it is documentation/metadata. Reachability needs docker run -p (or -P, which uses EXPOSE).

cards.front: What invalidates the Docker build cache?
cards.back: The first instruction whose inputs changed invalidates its layer and every layer after it — hence order least-changed first.

cards.front: Why COPY requirements.txt before COPY . . ?
cards.back: Dependencies change rarely, so the expensive pip-install layer stays cached across code edits; only the final cheap COPY re-runs.

cards.front: Should you use python:latest as a base? Why not?
cards.back: No — latest floats, so rebuilds may pull a different runtime. Pin the tag (python:3.12-slim) like any other dependency.

cards.front: Where does data a container must keep belong?
cards.back: In a volume, not the container's writable layer — the writable layer dies with the container.

quiz.q: Two containers run from the same image. What do they share on disk?
choices: Nothing — each gets a full copy
The read-only image layers; each has only its own thin writable layer
quiz.explain: Image layers are shared read-only; starting a second container costs only its thin writable layer.

quiz.q: Panel: what does RUN do in a Dockerfile?
choices: It runs a command when the container starts
Each RUN executes against the previous layer and commits the diff as a new read-only layer
quiz.explain: One RUN = one new immutable layer stacked on the previous one; docker history proves it.

quiz.q: A Dockerfile has three RUN instructions. How many layers do they add?
choices: Zero — RUN does not create layers
quiz.explain: Each RUN commits its own layer regardless of caching; caching only decides whether the layer is rebuilt or reused.

quiz.q: Why is 'RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*' one RUN instead of three?
choices: Split across RUNs, the package lists would persist in an intermediate layer despite the later rm
quiz.explain: Layers are immutable — a later rm cannot shrink an earlier layer, so cleanup must happen in the same RUN that created the files.

quiz.q: When should you use ADD instead of COPY?
choices: Almost never; COPY for files, RUN curl + checksum for remote artifacts
ADD is faster for large files
quiz.explain: ADD's magic (auto-extract, remote fetch without verification) hides behavior; explicit COPY/curl is reviewable.

quiz.q: ENTRYPOINT ["python","app.py"] and CMD ["--port","8080"]. What does 'docker run img --port 9090' execute?
choices: It errors — CMD cannot be overridden
quiz.explain: Run arguments replace CMD defaults and are appended to the fixed ENTRYPOINT.

quiz.q: Why is shell-form CMD a problem for docker stop?
choices: SIGTERM goes to the /bin/sh wrapper, not your app, so graceful shutdown fails
quiz.explain: The shell wrapper becomes PID 1 and does not forward signals; exec form runs your binary as PID 1 directly.

quiz.q: COPY . . comes before RUN pip install. Every code edit triggers a full pip reinstall. Fix?
choices: COPY requirements.txt and RUN pip install first, then COPY . . last
quiz.explain: Order least-changed first: the rarely-changing dependency layer stays cached while code edits only re-run the final COPY.

quiz.q: Does EXPOSE 8080 make the port reachable from the host?
choices: No — it is metadata; use docker run -p to publish
quiz.explain: EXPOSE documents intent; publishing is a separate runtime flag.

items.prompt: Write the first two lines of a Dockerfile for a Python app pinned to 3.12-slim with workdir /app.
items.answer:

WORKDIR /app

items.prompt: Order these for cache efficiency: COPY . ., RUN pip install -r requirements.txt, COPY requirements.txt .
items.answer: COPY requirements.txt . → RUN pip install -r requirements.txt → COPY . .
items.explain: Least-changed first: dependency layer stays cached across code edits.

items.prompt: Install curl in the image without leaving apt lists behind. Write the RUN.
items.answer: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
items.explain: Single RUN so cleanup lands in the same layer as the lists; && aborts on failure.

items.prompt: Set a fixed executable python app.py with overridable default arg --port 8080, exec form.
items.answer:
ENTRYPOINT ["python", "app.py"]
CMD ["--port", "8080"]
items.explain: ENTRYPOINT is fixed; CMD defaults are appended and replaceable at docker run.

items.prompt: How do you prove an image's layer count and sizes?
items.answer: docker history <image> — one row per layer with sizes.
items.explain: History exposes the layer stack the Dockerfile recipe produced.

items.prompt: A build copies the local .venv into the image. What is wrong and what is the fix?
items.answer: Bloat and possible secret leakage; fix with .dockerignore excluding .venv (and .git).
items.explain: Build context hygiene — covered fully in M23.

items.prompt: docker run myimg /bin/bash starts a shell instead of the app. Which instruction did the author use, and what is the alternative?
items.answer: They used CMD (fully replaceable); ENTRYPOINT would have kept the app as the fixed executable.
items.explain: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT semantics in one symptom.

items.prompt: Define image and container in one sentence each.
items.answer: Image: immutable template of read-only layers plus metadata. Container: a running instance — those layers plus a thin writable layer and an isolated process.
items.explain: Template versus instance; the class/object analogy.

items.prompt: You docker exec into a container, create /tmp/data.txt, then remove the container. Where is the file?
items.answer: Gone — it lived in the container's writable layer, which dies with the container.
items.explain: Writable layers are ephemeral; volumes persist.

items.prompt: Which is the unit of distribution and which the unit of execution?
items.answer: Image: distribution (registries, scanning, promotion). Container: execution (start, stop, replace).
items.explain: You ship images; you run containers.

items.prompt: Why does 'works on my machine' die with images?
items.answer: The image carries OS libs, runtime, and pinned deps — CI-tested bytes are identical to production bytes.
items.explain: The environment ships with the artifact.

items.prompt: docker images shows healthcheck v1 at 148MB. You start 5 containers. Roughly how much extra disk?
items.answer: Almost nothing beyond 148MB — the image layers are shared; only five thin writable layers are added.
items.explain: Layer sharing makes containers cheap to start.

items.prompt: Name two reasons to prefer official base images.
items.answer: They are maintained/scanned/documented, and their tags are trustworthy for pinning.
items.explain: Supply-chain hygiene starts at FROM.

items.prompt: How should base-image updates be handled?
items.answer: Deliberately: schedule refreshes, test, re-pin — never let a floating tag change the runtime silently.
items.explain: The base is a dependency with the same discipline as pip pins.

title: Multi-Stage Builds & Image Optimization
summary: Shrink images dramatically with multi-stage builds, minimal bases, and .dockerignore — and master the panel's favorite Docker questions: the whiteout lesson, the 'echo hello' trap, and measuring what each layer costs.
objectives: Write multi-stage Dockerfiles that keep build tooling out of the runtime image.
Choose minimal base images and justify the trade-offs.

Explain the whiteout lesson: deleting files in a later layer does not shrink the image.

notes.title: Multi-stage builds: ship the artifact, not the toolchain
notes.body:
A multi-stage Dockerfile uses multiple FROM instructions: early stages build the artifact with the full toolchain, and the final stage copies only the artifact into a lean runtime image. Everything left behind in earlier stages never ships. Worked example — the Go port-checker from M21:

# Build stage: full toolchain
FROM golang:1.23 AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /portcheck .

# Runtime stage: only the binary
FROM scratch
COPY --from=builder /portcheck /portcheck
ENTRYPOINT ["/portcheck"]

Solution walkthrough: the builder stage (hundreds of MB: compiler, module cache) compiles a static binary; the final stage starts FROM scratch — literally empty — and copies in just /portcheck. The published image is a few MB: no Go toolchain, no source, no module cache. COPY --from=builder is the bridge between stages, and naming stages with AS makes the intent readable. The same pattern serves compiled languages and frontend builds alike (node:slim builds the bundle, nginx:alpine serves it). Panel framing: "multi-stage separates build-time dependencies from runtime dependencies at the image layer." Without it, teams ship compilers and caches to production — larger attack surface, slower pulls, slower deploys. Verify the win with docker images: compare the builder-stage size against the final.

notes.title: Minimal bases: scratch, distroless, alpine, slim
notes.body:
The base image sets your floor for size and attack surface, and the options form a spectrum. scratch is empty — nothing but what you copy in; ideal for static binaries, but there is no shell for debugging. Distroless images add just a runtime (language libs, CA certs) with no shell or package manager — a strong default for dynamic languages. Alpine is a tiny full Linux (~5MB) with a shell and apk — great for debugging, though its musl libc occasionally surprises glibc-linked binaries. Slim variants (python:3.12-slim) drop the compiler toolchain but keep a familiar Debian userland. Worked example of the decision:

# Needs a shell for debugging and apk for packages:
FROM python:3.12-alpine
# Static Go binary, no shell needed:
FROM scratch

There is no universally right answer — only trade-offs to defend. Smaller base means faster pulls (matters enormously at scale: a 1GB image pulled by 500 nodes is 500GB of transfer), fewer packages to patch, and fewer CVEs for scanners to flag. But an image you cannot debug at 3 a.m. has its own cost, which is why many teams standardize on slim/distroless for production and keep a debug variant with a shell. The panel expects you to name the spectrum and argue a choice for a given workload, not to recite a favorite.

notes.title: .dockerignore: control the build context
notes.body:
docker build sends the entire build context directory to the daemon before the first instruction runs — including your .git history, local virtualenvs, .env files with secrets, and editor swap files. .dockerignore filters that context, exactly like .gitignore filters commits. Worked example for a Python project:

.git
.venv
__pycache__
*.pyc
.env
*.log
Dockerfile

Solution walkthrough: .git alone can be hundreds of MB — excluding it slashes context transfer time on every build; .venv and __pycache__ are local artifacts that must never ship; .env exclusion is a security control, because anything COPY . . would otherwise bake secrets into a layer (and layers are forever — a secret in any layer is in the image permanently, retrievable with docker save). Two verifications: run docker build and watch the "transferring context" size drop, and audit with a temporary RUN find / -name "*.env" in a test build. Professional rule: every repo with a Dockerfile gets a .dockerignore from day one, reviewed like code — because the build context is an input to your supply chain, and unfiltered inputs are how secrets leak into registries.

notes.title: The whiteout lesson: later deletes do not shrink earlier layers
notes.body:
This is the panel's favorite Docker trap, so learn the mechanism: layers are immutable, and deleting a file in a later layer only adds a whiteout marker that hides the file in the merged view — the bytes remain in the earlier layer, and the image stays the same size. Worked example — the wrong way:

FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
RUN dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/blob bs=1M count=100
RUN rm /tmp/blob

Build it and run docker images: the image is ~100MB larger than the base, even though /tmp/blob no longer exists in the running container. The rm layer contains only a whiteout file saying "/tmp/blob is deleted"; the 100MB of zeros sit untouched in the previous layer. Now the right way — one RUN:

RUN dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/blob bs=1M count=100 && rm /tmp/blob

The file is created and deleted inside the same layer commit, so it never persists — image size unchanged. This is exactly why the M22 apt-get pattern chains update, install, and cleanup with && in one RUN. The panel question "does removing files in a later layer reduce image size?" expects: no — whiteout hides but does not delete; only same-layer cleanup (or multi-stage, or squashing) actually shrinks the image. Verify any claim with docker history: the layer sizes do not lie.

notes.title: The 'echo hello' trap: replacing cleanup grows the image
notes.body:
A panel variant of the whiteout lesson: take a Dockerfile whose RUN does install-then-cleanup, replace the cleanup step with RUN echo hello, and ask what happens to the image size. Worked example:

# Original
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Modified: cleanup replaced
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
RUN echo hello

Solution: the image grows by the size of /var/lib/apt/lists/* (tens of MB). Walkthrough: the first RUN's layer permanently contains the downloaded package lists; the second RUN adds a tiny layer with hello's output and changes nothing about the first. Replacing cleanup with an unrelated command does not remove the files — layers are append-only history. The general principle: every byte written by a RUN lives in that RUN's layer forever, so cleanup must happen in the same RUN that created the mess, joined with && so failures abort before the commit. Related panel follow-up: "how would you actually shrink it?" — rewrite as a single RUN with the rm restored, or restructure with multi-stage so the package manager never appears in the final image at all. When optimizing, always measure before and after with docker images; intuition about sizes is unreliable, the numbers are not.

notes.title: Measuring: docker images, history, and system df
notes.body:
Optimization without measurement is guessing. Three commands form the measurement toolkit. docker images shows repository, tag, and total size per image — your before/after scoreboard. docker history <image> breaks that total into per-layer rows with sizes and the creating command — your profiler, showing exactly which instruction costs what. docker system df reports overall disk usage: images, containers, build cache, and how much is reclaimable. Worked example — the optimization loop:

$ docker build -t api:naive -f Dockerfile.naive .
$ docker build -t api:opt -f Dockerfile.opt .
$ docker images --format '{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}} {{.Size}}'
api:naive 1.12GB
api:opt 142MB
$ docker history api:naive --format '{{.CreatedBy}} {{.Size}}' | sort -k2 -h | tail -3

Solution walkthrough: the scoreboard proves the 8x win; the history tail names the three most expensive layers (usually a fat base, an uncached pip install, and a COPY of unfiltered context) — each maps to a fix from this module (minimal base, cache-ordered deps, .dockerignore). Workflow discipline: measure the naive build first, change one thing, rebuild, compare. docker system df -v goes deeper per-object when hunting a disk-full builder, and docker builder prune reclaims cache deliberately — never on a shared CI builder without coordination. Panels respect engineers who quote their numbers: "multi-stage took us from 1.1GB to 142MB" beats "we optimized the image."

cards.front: What is a multi-stage Dockerfile, and what problem does it solve?
cards.back: Multiple FROM stages: early stages build with the full toolchain, the final stage copies only the artifact in — build tooling never ships to production.

cards.front: What does COPY --from=builder /portcheck /portcheck do?
cards.back: Copies the built binary from the named builder stage into the final stage's filesystem.

cards.front: Order these bases by size/simplicity: scratch, distroless, alpine, slim.
cards.back: scratch (empty) < distroless (runtime only, no shell) < alpine (tiny full Linux) < slim (Debian minus toolchain). Smaller = faster pulls, fewer CVEs, harder to debug.

cards.front: What does .dockerignore do, and name three things that belong in it.
cards.back: Filters the build context sent to the daemon: .git, .venv, .env (secrets must never bake into layers).

cards.front: Panel: does removing a file in a later layer shrink the image?
cards.back: No — the delete only adds a whiteout marker hiding the file; the bytes remain in the earlier immutable layer and the size is unchanged.

cards.front: How do you actually remove the bytes, then?
cards.back: Create and delete in the same RUN (&& chained), or restructure with multi-stage so the files never enter the final image.

cards.front: Panel: you replace a RUN's cleanup step with 'RUN echo hello'. What happens to image size?
cards.back: It grows — the files the cleanup would have removed persist in the earlier layer; the echo layer changes nothing about them.

cards.front: Which three commands measure image/layer/disk usage?
cards.back: docker images (per-image totals), docker history (per-layer sizes + creating command), docker system df (overall reclaimable usage).

cards.front: Why is a secret in any image layer a permanent leak?
cards.back: Layers are immutable and ship with the image — anyone with the image can extract the layer's bytes (e.g. via docker save).

cards.front: A 1GB image is pulled by 500 nodes. Why does base-image size matter?
cards.back: That is ~500GB of transfer plus slower rollouts — minimal bases directly cut pull time, disk, and patch surface at scale.

cards.front: What is the optimization loop you should follow?
cards.back: Measure the naive build (docker images/history), change one thing, rebuild, compare — quote the numbers.

cards.front: When is alpine a risky base choice?
cards.back: Its musl libc can surprise glibc-linked binaries — test compatibility; otherwise it is a fine tiny base with a shell.

quiz.q: What is the core benefit of a multi-stage Dockerfile?
choices: Build tooling stays in early stages; the final image contains only the runtime artifact
It removes the need for a base image
quiz.explain: Stages separate build-time from runtime dependencies at the image layer — compilers and caches never ship.

quiz.q: In a Go multi-stage build, why can the final stage be FROM scratch?
choices: A static Go binary needs no OS userland — just copy the binary in
quiz.explain: CGO_ENABLED=0 produces a static binary with no libc dependency, so an empty base suffices.

quiz.q: Which .dockerignore entry is a security control, and why?
choices: .env — otherwise secrets bake into immutable layers permanently
quiz.explain: Anything copied into a layer ships forever; .env exclusion keeps secrets out of the image supply chain.

quiz.q: Panel: RUN downloads a 100MB file, and a later RUN deletes it. Final image size impact?
choices: +100MB — the whiteout hides the file but the bytes persist in the earlier layer
quiz.explain: Immutable layers: the later rm only adds a whiteout marker; measure with docker history to see the layer still holding 100MB.

quiz.q: How do you make the 100MB actually disappear?
choices: Download and delete in the same RUN, or use multi-stage
quiz.explain: Same-layer cleanup never commits the bytes; multi-stage keeps them out of the final image entirely.

quiz.q: Panel: replacing '&& rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*' with 'RUN echo hello' — image size?
choices: Grows by the apt lists size — the cleanup no longer happens and layers are append-only
quiz.explain: The package lists persist in their layer; the echo layer cannot remove them.

quiz.q: docker history shows one 900MB layer from 'COPY . .'. Most likely cause and fix?
choices: Base image is fat — change FROM
quiz.explain: A giant COPY layer means the context carried junk; .dockerignore is the fix.

quiz.q: Why might a team standardize on distroless for production but keep a debug variant?
choices: Distroless minimizes attack surface; the debug variant keeps a shell for 3 a.m. troubleshooting
quiz.explain: The trade-off is explicit: minimal surface in prod, debuggability when incidents strike.

quiz.q: Before/after: 1.12GB → 142MB via multi-stage. What proved the win?
choices: docker images size comparison plus docker history identifying the expensive layers
quiz.explain: images gives the scoreboard; history profiles which layers cost what — measurement, not intuition.

items.prompt: Panel: 'Does removing files in a later layer reduce image size?' Give the full answer.
items.answer: No. Layers are immutable; the delete adds only a whiteout marker hiding the file, while the bytes persist in the earlier layer. Prove it with docker history showing the layer size unchanged.
items.explain: Mechanism (whiteout) + proof (history) is the complete panel answer.

items.prompt: Panel: 'You replaced the cleanup step with RUN echo hello. What happens to size?'
items.answer: It grows by whatever the cleanup would have removed — layers are append-only, so the echo layer cannot delete the earlier layer's files.
items.explain: The trap variant: cleanup must happen in the creating RUN.

items.prompt: Write the correct apt-get RUN that leaves no package lists behind.
items.answer: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
items.explain: Single RUN, && chaining so failure aborts before commit, cleanup in the same layer.

items.prompt: Why does multi-stage beat even perfect single-stage cleanup for compiled apps?
items.answer: The compiler, source, and caches never enter the final image at all — cleanup can only remove files, multi-stage removes whole toolchains.
items.explain: Qualitative difference, not just tidier layers.

items.prompt: Your final stage is FROM scratch. What must be true of the binary?
items.answer: It must be fully static (e.g. CGO_ENABLED=0 for Go) — scratch has no libc, no shell, nothing.
items.explain: Scratch works only when the artifact has zero runtime dependencies.

items.prompt: Name the measurement commands and what each tells you.
items.answer: docker images: per-image totals (scoreboard). docker history: per-layer sizes and creating command (profiler). docker system df: overall reclaimable disk.
items.explain: Scoreboard, profiler, janitor.

items.prompt: A reviewer says 'just use python:latest, it is always patched.' Your response?
items.answer: Floating tags break reproducibility — rebuilds silently change the runtime. Pin the base tag and schedule deliberate, tested refreshes instead.
items.explain: Same pinning discipline as pip, applied to the base image.

items.prompt: Sketch a multi-stage Dockerfile for a Go app: builder and scratch final.
items.answer: FROM golang:1.23 AS builder → WORKDIR, COPY go.mod, RUN go mod download, COPY ., RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /app .; then FROM scratch → COPY --from=builder /app /app → ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
items.explain: Toolchain in builder, static binary only in final.

items.prompt: What does AS builder enable?
items.answer: Names the stage so later COPY --from=builder can reference it — readable and explicit.
items.explain: Named stages are the bridge mechanism.

items.prompt: Write a .dockerignore for a Python repo and justify each line.
items.answer: .git (huge history), .venv (local env), __pycache__/*.pyc (build junk), .env (secrets must never layer), *.log, Dockerfile
items.explain: Size, hygiene, and the security control.

items.prompt: How do you verify .dockerignore worked?
items.answer: Watch the 'transferring context' size drop on build, and audit with a test RUN find for excluded names.
items.explain: Measure the context, not just the image.

items.prompt: Frontend pattern: node builds, nginx serves. Sketch the stages.
items.answer: FROM node:slim AS build → COPY, RUN npm ci && npm run build; FROM nginx:alpine → COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
items.explain: Same pattern, different runtimes — toolchain never ships.

items.prompt: When would you NOT use scratch for the final stage?
items.answer: When you need a shell, CA certs, or a language runtime at debug/run time — then distroless/alpine/slim.
items.explain: Scratch is for fully static artifacts; debuggability has value.

items.prompt: docker system df shows 40GB reclaimable on a shared CI builder. What do you do?
items.answer: Coordinate first — docker builder prune affects everyone's cache; never prune a shared builder unilaterally.
items.explain: Cache is shared infrastructure; pruning is a team decision.

handsOnLab.title: Three builds, one scoreboard
handsOnLab.brief: You will build naive, cleaned-up, and multi-stage variants of the same app, measure each with docker images and docker history, demonstrate the whiteout effect live, and record the numbers.
steps: Set up: mkdir opt-lab && cd opt-lab; create app.py (a trivial HTTP server or the M19 healthcheck) and requirements.txt with one pinned dep.
Write Dockerfile.naive: FROM python:3.12, separate RUNs for apt update/install (install curl) with no cleanup, COPY . . first then pip install (bad cache order), no .dockerignore.
Build naive: docker build -t opt:naive -f Dockerfile.naive . ; record docker images size for opt:naive.
Write Dockerfile.clean: FROM python:3.12-slim, single chained apt RUN with cleanup, COPY requirements.txt + pip install before COPY . ., plus a .dockerignore excluding .git/__pycache__/*.pyc.
Build clean: docker build -t opt:clean -f Dockerfile.clean . ; record size; compare with naive.

Whiteout demo: add to the naive variant 'RUN dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/blob bs=1M count=50' followed by 'RUN rm /tmp/blob'; rebuild and show via docker history that the layer (and image size) still carries ~50MB.
Echo-hello demo: in a copy of the clean Dockerfile, replace the apt cleanup with a separate 'RUN echo hello'; rebuild and record the size increase.
Multi-stage: write Dockerfile.multi for a static Go hello (or reuse portcheck): golang builder → scratch final; build and record the tiny final size.
Profile: run docker history on each tag, identify the single most expensive layer per variant, and map it to its fix.
Write sizes.md: the four image sizes, the whiteout/echo-hello deltas, and the one-paragraph whiteout explanation in your own words.
handsOnLab.deliverable: Dockerfile.naive, Dockerfile.clean, Dockerfile.multi, .dockerignore, and sizes.md with all measurements and the whiteout explanation.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: sizes.md shows clean < naive, multi smallest; whiteout demo proves the rm layer did not shrink the image; echo-hello variant measurably larger than clean.

mockTask.q: Panel: 'Your production image is 1.1GB for a Go microservice. Walk me through shrinking it.'
choices: Add RUN rm -rf on the build tools in the final layer
Multi-stage: compile in a golang builder stage, copy the static binary into a scratch final stage; verify with docker images/history
Compress the image with gzip before pushing
Split the app into more layers
mockTask.explain: Later-layer deletes cannot shrink earlier layers (whiteout); multi-stage keeps the toolchain out of the final image entirely — the only approach that actually removes the bytes. Measurement with docker images/history proves the win.

title: Docker Networking, Volumes & Compose
summary: Connect containers with bridge networks and DNS-based service discovery, persist data with volumes versus bind mounts, and define multi-service stacks in an original docker-compose file you bring up yourself.
objectives: Explain bridge networking and how containers resolve each other by name.
Publish container ports to the host with -p and describe what EXPOSE does not do.
Compare host, bridge, and none network modes and choose appropriately.
Contrast named volumes with bind mounts for data persistence.
Write and operate a multi-service docker-compose stack from scratch.

notes.title: Bridge networks: isolation plus automatic DNS
notes.body:
The default docker0 bridge — and any user-defined bridge network — gives each container its own IP on a private subnet while Docker runs an embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11 inside every container. The practical magic: on a user-defined bridge network, containers resolve each other by name (or by Compose service name) with zero configuration. Worked example:

$ docker network create appnet
$ docker run -d --name cache --network appnet redis:alpine
$ docker run -d --name web --network appnet nginx:alpine
$ docker exec web wget -qO- --timeout=2 http://cache:6379 | head -c 40

The wget reaches the Redis container via the hostname "cache" — Docker's DNS resolved it to the container's bridge IP, and the TCP connection succeeded (Redis replies with a protocol error to HTTP, which is exactly the proof of connectivity we want). On the default bridge this name resolution does NOT work — only user-defined networks get automatic DNS, which is why docker compose creates one per project automatically. Inspect the plumbing with docker network inspect appnet: it lists each attached container, its IPv4 address, and aliases. The mental model: a bridge network is a virtual switch; DNS is the phone book; together they let services find each other by stable names even as container IPs churn across restarts — the same service-discovery idea Kubernetes builds on.

notes.title: Publishing ports: -p and what EXPOSE does not do
notes.body:
A container's ports are private to its network by default. docker run -p HOST:CONTAINER publishes a container port on a host interface, creating the NAT rule that lets outside traffic in. Worked example:

$ docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name web nginx:alpine
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://localhost:8080
200

The container listens on 80 (per its EXPOSE 80 metadata); the host forwards localhost:8080 to it. Variants: -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 binds only the loopback (safer for admin UIs you do not want LAN-exposed); -p 8080:80 with no host IP binds all interfaces; -P publishes every EXPOSEd port on random host ports. Three sharp edges. One: EXPOSE alone publishes nothing — it is documentation (M22); without -p the port stays unreachable from the host. Two: publishing the same host port twice fails — the second container errors on bind, a classic "works alone, breaks together" defect. Three: -p on the default bridge plus container-to-container traffic means your app should listen on 0.0.0.0 inside the container, not 127.0.0.1 — binding localhost inside the container accepts only the container's own loopback, and published-port traffic arrives on the container's eth0. When curl fails, check in order: is the app listening on 0.0.0.0, is the port published, is a host firewall blocking it.

notes.title: Host and none: the other network modes
notes.body:
Bridge is the default, but two other modes matter. Host mode (--network host) removes network isolation entirely: the container shares the host's network namespace, so a process listening on port 80 binds the host's port 80 directly — no -p needed, no NAT overhead. Use it for network-monitoring agents or ultra-low-latency services; avoid it for ordinary apps because any port conflict hits the host and isolation is gone. Note it is a Linux-only feature — Docker Desktop's VM makes host mode behave differently, a favorite interview gotcha. None mode (--network none) gives the container a loopback interface and nothing else: no external connectivity at all. Use it for untrusted batch jobs or security-sensitive one-shot tasks where network exfiltration must be impossible. Worked comparison:

$ docker run --rm --network host nginx:alpine  # binds host's port 80 directly
$ docker run --rm --network none alpine ping -c1 8.8.8.8  # fails: no route

Decision guide: bridge for normal multi-container apps (isolation + DNS), host for agents that must see host traffic, none for compute-only sandboxes. Panels ask "when would you use host networking?" expecting the monitoring/low-latency answer plus the port-conflict and Linux-only caveats — not "for speed" alone.

notes.title: Volumes vs bind mounts: where persistent data lives
notes.body:
Container filesystems are ephemeral (M22) — data that must survive needs storage outside the container's writable layer. Named volumes (-v cache-data:/data) are Docker-managed storage in Docker's own directory: portable, easy to back up, and the right default for databases and caches. Bind mounts (-v /host/path:/data) map a specific host directory into the container: transparent and editable from the host, ideal for mounting source code into dev containers or config files. Worked example — proving a named volume persists:

$ docker run -d --name cache -v cache-data:/data redis:alpine
$ docker exec cache redis-cli set greeting hello
OK
$ docker exec cache redis-cli save
OK
$ docker rm -f cache
$ docker run -d --name cache2 -v cache-data:/data redis:alpine
$ docker exec cache2 redis-cli get greeting
hello

Solution walkthrough: the data lived in the cache-data volume, not in either container's writable layer, so destroying the first container lost nothing; the SAVE forced Redis to flush to /data/dump.rdb before removal. Contrast with anonymous volumes (a bare -v /data with no name): they persist too, but with random hash names that accumulate as orphans — always name your volumes. Inspect with docker volume ls and docker volume inspect; reclaim with docker volume prune (destructive — confirm nothing needed first). Rule: volumes for data, bind mounts for code/config you edit on the host.

notes.title: Compose: the whole stack in one file
notes.body:
docker compose turns a multi-container system into a single declarative YAML file: services, networks, and volumes defined together and managed as one unit (up, down, logs, ps). Here is an original two-service stack — a web frontend plus a Redis cache — of the kind you will run in the lab:

services:
  web:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    networks:
      - appnet
    depends_on:
      - cache
  cache:
    image: redis:alpine
    volumes:
      - cache-data:/data
    networks:
      - appnet

networks:
  appnet:
    driver: bridge

volumes:
  cache-data:

Solution walkthrough, top to bottom: services defines the two containers; web publishes host 8080 to container 80; both join the user-defined bridge appnet, so web resolves the hostname "cache" via Docker DNS with no extra config; depends_on orders startup (web starts after cache — note: it orders startup, it does NOT wait for Redis to be ready; readiness needs a healthcheck or wait-for script); cache mounts the named volume at /data for persistence. Networks and volumes sections declare the shared resources once. docker compose up -d brings up the project (named after the directory); docker compose ps, logs, and exec operate per service; docker compose down stops and removes containers but KEEPS volumes, while down -v destroys them too — know the difference before typing.

notes.title: Operating the stack: the daily compose commands
notes.body:
Writing the file is half the skill; operating it is the other half. The daily command set, each with its purpose. docker compose up -d builds (if needed) and starts everything detached; add --build to force a rebuild after Dockerfile changes — without it, Compose reuses the old image and your fix silently does not deploy, a classic "but I changed the code" incident. docker compose ps shows service state at a glance; docker compose logs -f web tails one service's logs; docker compose exec cache redis-cli ping runs a command in the running container (PONG proves Redis is up). Worked debugging session:

$ docker compose up -d
$ docker compose ps
NAME            STATUS
lab-web-1       Up
lab-cache-1     Up
$ docker compose exec cache redis-cli ping
PONG
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://localhost:8080
200

Every layer verified: both services up, cache answering, web reachable through the published port. For teardown, docker compose down removes containers and the project network but preserves named volumes (data survives); docker compose down -v also deletes volumes (data destroyed — the nuclear option for a fresh start). Two production notes: pin image tags in compose files (redis:alpine is a floating tag — prefer redis:7-alpine after verifying), and keep secrets out of the YAML — use env_file pointing at an untracked .env, never commit credentials into the compose file.

cards.front: How do containers on a user-defined bridge resolve each other?
cards.back: Docker's embedded DNS (127.0.0.11) resolves container/service names automatically — but only on user-defined networks, not the default bridge.

cards.front: What does 'docker run -p 8080:80' do, precisely?
cards.back: Publishes the container's port 80 on host port 8080 via a NAT rule; without -p, EXPOSE alone leaves the port unreachable from the host.

cards.front: Your app binds 127.0.0.1 inside the container and curl to the published port fails. Why?
cards.back: Published traffic arrives on the container's eth0, not its loopback — the app must listen on 0.0.0.0.

cards.front: When is --network host the right choice, and what are its caveats?
cards.back: Network agents or ultra-low-latency services needing the host stack directly; caveats: no isolation, host port conflicts, Linux-only.

cards.front: What is --network none for?
cards.back: Containers with only loopback and no external networking — untrusted batch jobs or tasks where exfiltration must be impossible.

cards.front: Named volume vs bind mount — which for a database, which for dev source code?
cards.back: Named volume for the database (managed, portable, persists); bind mount for source code (editable live from the host).

cards.front: You removed a container but kept its named volume. Is the data still there?
cards.back: Yes — volumes live outside the container's writable layer; reattach the same volume name to a new container.

cards.front: What does depends_on guarantee — and what does it NOT guarantee?
cards.back: Startup order only — it does not wait for the dependency to be ready; use healthchecks or wait-for scripts for readiness.

cards.front: docker compose down vs docker compose down -v?
cards.back: down removes containers/network but keeps volumes (data survives); down -v also destroys volumes.

cards.front: You changed the Dockerfile but 'docker compose up -d' did not pick it up. Why?
cards.back: Compose reuses the existing image without --build — the fix never built. Use up -d --build after Dockerfile changes.

cards.front: How do you run a one-off command in a running Compose service?
cards.back: docker compose exec <service> <command>, e.g. docker compose exec cache redis-cli ping.

cards.front: Where do secrets belong in a Compose setup?
cards.back: In an untracked .env referenced via env_file — never hardcoded in the compose YAML.

quiz.q: Two containers on a user-defined bridge: web reaches the cache at hostname 'cache'. What provides this?
choices: Docker's embedded DNS on user-defined networks
quiz.explain: User-defined bridge networks get automatic DNS resolution by container/service name; the default bridge does not.

quiz.q: EXPOSE 80 is set but you ran without -p. Can the host reach the app?
choices: No — EXPOSE is metadata; publishing needs -p
quiz.explain: EXPOSE documents intent; reachability requires an explicit publish flag.

quiz.q: docker run -p 8080:80 fails with 'port is already allocated'. Cause and fix?
choices: Another process/container holds host port 8080 — stop it or choose a free host port
quiz.explain: Host ports are exclusive; find the holder (or pick another port).

quiz.q: When would you choose --network host?
choices: For every web app, for speed
For a network-monitoring agent needing the host's interfaces — accepting no isolation and Linux-only
quiz.explain: Host mode suits agents/sniffers; ordinary apps lose isolation and risk host port conflicts.

quiz.q: A batch job must not reach the network at all. Which mode?
quiz.explain: none gives only loopback — no external connectivity, so exfiltration is impossible.

quiz.q: Redis data must survive container replacement. Which mount?
choices: Named volume at /data — survives container removal and reattaches by name
No mount — the writable layer persists
quiz.explain: Named volumes persist outside the container lifecycle; the writable layer dies with the container.

quiz.q: In the compose file, what does depends_on: [cache] guarantee for web?
choices: cache is ready to serve before web starts
cache's container starts before web's — not readiness
quiz.explain: depends_on orders startup only; readiness needs healthchecks or wait-for logic.

quiz.q: After editing the Dockerfile, 'docker compose up -d' shows the old behavior. What was missed?
choices: A version bump in the YAML
quiz.explain: Compose reuses the cached image unless --build forces a rebuild.

quiz.q: You need a completely fresh start including wiping cached data. Which command?
quiz.explain: down -v also destroys named volumes; plain down preserves them.

items.prompt: Publish container port 80 on host port 8080, loopback only. Give the flag.
items.explain: Binding the host IP to loopback keeps the service off the LAN.

items.prompt: From container web, prove DNS resolves container cache on their shared network.
items.answer: docker exec web wget -qO- --timeout=2 http://cache:6379 (a Redis protocol-error reply proves name resolution + TCP).
items.explain: Any successful TCP to the hostname proves Docker DNS worked.

items.prompt: List containers on network appnet with their IPs. Give the command.
items.answer: docker network inspect appnet
items.explain: Shows attached containers, IPv4 addresses, and aliases.

items.prompt: curl to a published port fails but the app is up. Name three checks in order.
items.answer: App listening on 0.0.0.0 (not 127.0.0.1); port actually published (-p); host firewall allowing it.
items.explain: Inside-out debugging: bind address, publish rule, firewall.

items.prompt: When is host networking justified, and what do you give up?
items.answer: Agents needing host interfaces or extreme low latency; you give up isolation, risk host port conflicts, and it is Linux-only.
items.explain: The complete trade-off, not just 'speed'.

items.prompt: A security review demands a PDF renderer with no network. Which mode and flag?
items.answer: --network none — loopback only, exfiltration impossible.
items.explain: None mode is the sandbox answer.

items.prompt: Why does name resolution fail on the default bridge?
items.answer: Automatic embedded DNS exists only on user-defined networks; the default bridge predates the feature.
items.explain: Always create a network (or let Compose) for multi-container apps.

items.prompt: Run redis with a named volume at /data. Give the docker run.
items.answer: docker run -d --name cache -v cache-data:/data redis:alpine
items.explain: Named volume cache-data mounted at the data dir.

items.prompt: Prove the volume (not the container) holds the data.
items.answer: Write a key, redis-cli save, remove the container, start a new one on the same volume, read the key back.
items.explain: Data surviving container replacement proves volume persistence.

items.prompt: When do you choose a bind mount over a named volume?
items.answer: For host-editable content: dev source code, config files you iterate on — not for database data.
items.explain: Bind mounts are for the edit loop; volumes are for data.

items.prompt: Write the compose services block for web (nginx:alpine, 8080:80) depending on cache.
items.answer:
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports: ['8080:80']
    depends_on: [cache]
items.explain: Service, image, published port, startup ordering.

items.prompt: Declare the shared bridge network and named volume in compose.
items.answer:
networks:
  appnet:
    driver: bridge
volumes:
  cache-data:
items.explain: Top-level networks/volumes sections declare shared resources once.

items.prompt: Tail web's logs and ping Redis through compose. Give both commands.
items.answer: docker compose logs -f web && docker compose exec cache redis-cli ping
items.explain: logs per service; exec runs one-off commands in a running service.

items.prompt: A teammate committed AWS keys in the compose file. What now?
items.answer: Move to untracked .env + env_file, rotate the exposed keys immediately — committed secrets are compromised.
items.explain: Same rule as code: committed secrets are burned secrets.

handsOnLab.title: Multi-service stack: web + cache
handsOnLab.brief: You will write an original docker-compose stack (nginx web + Redis cache on a custom bridge with a named volume), prove DNS service discovery, prove volume persistence across container replacement, and practice the full operate cycle.
steps: Set up: mkdir compose-lab && cd compose-lab.
Write compose.yaml exactly as the services/networks/volumes example in the notes (web: nginx:alpine on 8080:80, cache: redis:alpine with cache-data:/data, both on appnet, web depends_on cache).
Bring it up: docker compose up -d, then docker compose ps — both services Up.
Prove the cache: docker compose exec cache redis-cli ping — expect PONG.
Prove DNS discovery: docker compose exec web wget -qO- --timeout=2 http://cache:6379 | head -c 60 — a Redis protocol-error reply proves the hostname 'cache' resolved and TCP connected.
Prove publishing: curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:8080 — expect 200 from nginx.

Prove persistence: docker compose exec cache redis-cli set labkey persisted && docker compose exec cache redis-cli save; then docker compose rm -f -s cache; docker compose up -d; then docker compose exec cache redis-cli get labkey — expect 'persisted'.
Observe ordering limits: docker compose logs cache | head -20 and note that depends_on ordered startup but did not wait for readiness.
Teardown keeping data: docker compose down, then docker volume ls — cache-data still present; bring the stack up again and re-read labkey.
Nuclear teardown: docker compose down -v, confirm the volume is gone, and write stack.md documenting each proof and the down vs down -v difference.
handsOnLab.deliverable: compose.yaml and stack.md with the DNS, publishing, persistence, and teardown proofs.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: PONG from redis-cli; Redis error-reply via hostname 'cache'; 200 from localhost:8080; labkey survives container replacement and plain down, but not down -v.

mockTask.q: Panel: 'Two containers need to talk, data must survive restarts, and the web port must be reachable. Sketch it.'
choices: Both on the default bridge, data in the writable layer, EXPOSE 80
User-defined bridge network (DNS by service name), named volume for data, -p 8080:80 publishing, app listening on 0.0.0.0
--network host for both, bind-mount /tmp, no published ports
One container with both processes, --network none
mockTask.explain: User-defined bridge gives DNS discovery; named volumes survive container replacement; -p publishes explicitly (EXPOSE alone does nothing); 0.0.0.0 binding is required for published traffic. The other options lose data, discovery, or isolation.
